Melting noncoplanar order on the square-kagome lattice: Chiral, flat-band, and staggered spin liquids from projective symmetry

Harsh Raj Affiliation: Department of Physics, Indian Institute of Technology Madras, Chennai 600036, India    Atanu Maity Affiliation: Institut für Theoretische Physik und Astrophysik and Würzburg-Dresden Cluster of Excellence ctd.qmat, Julius-Maximilians-Universität Würzburg, Am Hubland, Campus Süd, Würzburg 97074, Germany Affiliation: Department of Physics, Indian Institute of Technology Madras, Chennai 600036, India    Yasir Iqbal Email: yiqbal@physics.iitm.ac.in Affiliation: Department of Physics, Indian Institute of Technology Madras, Chennai 600036, India
Abstract

Noncoplanar magnetic orders carry a scalar spin chirality, and their melting by quantum fluctuations has been proposed as a route to chiral spin liquids. We ask what this route can produce on the square-kagome lattice, where couplings across the octagons stabilize noncoplanar cuboc and conical orders. We classify the fermionic spin liquids of this lattice by their projective symmetry groups, identify the symmetry class into which each noncoplanar order would melt, and compare candidate states with Gutzwiller-projected wave functions. A magnetic selection rule constrains the route: the chirality of every cuboc and conical order alternates in space, so a liquid that keeps the symmetry of its parent order has zero Chern number and no spontaneous thermal Hall response. A Chern state can descend only from uniformly chiral orders, and the regular ones we find need ferromagnetic bow-tie couplings. The energetics do not favor a chiral liquid either: among the projected wave functions we compare, a cuboc1-ordered state is lowest for strong cross-octagon couplings, and nonchiral states, a valence-bond crystal or a time-reversal-symmetric liquid, for weaker ones. The two inequivalent site orbits shape the spinons: a relative time-reversal sign between them pins flat bands to the Fermi level, and because the translations of p​4​m​mp4mm are not commutators, staggered chiral liquids exist, which are absent on sixfold-symmetric lattices.

I Introduction

Noncoplanar magnetic orders carry a scalar spin chirality, and when quantum fluctuations melt such an order the chirality may survive in a chiral spin liquid, a state without magnetic order that breaks time reversal and can carry chiral edge modes and a thermal Hall response [47, 115]. Quantum melting of noncoplanar orders has been studied as a general route to such liquids [38]. We call the route in which the liquid keeps the magnetic symmetry of its parent order the inherited route, and the parent the melted order. On the kagome lattice, further-neighbor couplings stabilize cuboctahedral (cuboc) orders [19, 72], and a chiral liquid was proposed as their melted form [73]. Bosonic and fermionic mean-field and variational studies [74, 9, 8, 39] as well as density-matrix renormalization group and exact-diagonalization studies [28, 36, 27, 118] find chiral spin liquids near these orders, in the regions where classical ordered phases meet [118]. On the square-kagome lattice, couplings across the octagons stabilize cuboc and conical noncoplanar orders, and Gembé et al. proposed that their quantum melting could give chiral spin liquids [26]. Whether such a liquid keeps the symmetry of its melted order decides how it can be observed: a liquid whose chirality alternates in space has no spontaneous thermal Hall response, whereas a uniformly chiral liquid can have one. In this work, we address this question with the projective symmetry groups of fermionic spin liquids on the square-kagome lattice and with Gutzwiller-projected wave functions.

The square-kagome lattice, also called the squagome or shuriken lattice, is a network of corner-sharing triangles with coordination four [100, 111, 79]. It is the medial (line-graph) lattice of the square-octagon tiling [79], in the same way as the kagome lattice is the medial lattice of the honeycomb lattice, and its unit cell contains four triangles, one square, and one octagon. Its spin-1/21/2 Heisenberg antiferromagnet has a nonmagnetic ground state with a spin gap and many low-lying singlets [100, 90, 91]. Exact diagonalization of clusters up to 3636 sites gives a ground-state energy of about −0.440​J-0.440J per site and magnetization plateaus at 1/31/3 and 2/32/3 of saturation [79]. Numerical studies agree that it is a valence-bond crystal but differ on which one. Quantum dimer and resonating-valence-bond descriptions favor valence-bond crystals with resonating building blocks [94, 87], and variational Monte Carlo finds a pinwheel valence-bond crystal as an instability of a U⁡(1)U(1) Dirac spin liquid [4]. Tensor-network calculations find a loop-six valence-bond crystal at the isotropic point and a sequence of valence-bond crystals and Lieb ferrimagnets as the ratio of the two nearest-neighbor couplings varies [97, 44]. Schwinger-boson mean-field theory of the model with inequivalent bow-tie edges finds, besides ordered phases, a topological spin liquid with weak nematicity [63].

In a magnetic field the lattice shows magnetization plateaus and jumps [76, 34] and, near saturation, localized magnons on its flat magnon band [92, 16], and its classical Ising and Heisenberg models show reentrant disorder [83] and cuboc ground states with unusual magnetization curves [96, 93]. The lattice is realized, in decorated and distorted form, in copper minerals and their synthetic analogs. KCu6AlBiO4(SO4)5Cl shows no order down to 5858 mK and a gapless continuum [23], although nuclear magnetic resonance suggests a magnetic ground state with a small gap [29]. Na6Cu7BiO4(PO4)4[Cl,(OH)]3 shows no order down to 5050 mK [119, 56] and lies close to a magnetic instability in ab initio models [80, 110], whereas KCu7TeO4(SO4)5Cl orders at TN=3.2T_{N}=3.2 K [78, 71, 46].

In the parton description of a frustrated Heisenberg magnet the spin is represented by fermionic spinons coupled to an emergent gauge field [6, 5, 2, 116, 117]. Symmetric spin liquids are then distinguished by their projective symmetry group (PSG), the projective representation under which the spinons transform [116], and chiral spin liquids, in which time reversal and some lattice symmetries are broken while their products survive, are classified in the same framework [74, 8]. PSG classifications of fermionic spin liquids exist for many two-dimensional [116, 89, 121, 62, 8, 61, 60, 9, 15, 120, 70, 69, 95, 68, 105, 11, 67] and three-dimensional [104, 12, 58, 59, 98, 13, 57, 41, 45, 40, 14, 52] lattices, and the same framework classifies bosonic spinons in Schwinger-boson theory [112]. For the square-kagome lattice, the fermionic mean-field study of Astrakhantsev et al. classified U⁡(1)U(1) states by their nearest-neighbor fluxes, among them chiral states with flux π/2\pi/2 per triangle, and listed a PSG classification as an open problem [4].

We work in Abrikosov-fermion mean-field theory with spin-singlet and spin-triplet amplitudes on all twelve bond orbits up to the couplings J×J_{\times} and J+J_{+} across the octagons [26], where the triplet amplitudes describe the effect of spin–orbit coupling [17, 59]. The mean-field amplitudes are first treated as free parameters constrained only by the PSG, so that spectral types refer to regions of amplitude space. In a second step we solve the self-consistency equations of the Heisenberg model of Ref. [26] within each PSG manifold at representative points of its noncoplanar phases, and we compare Gutzwiller-projected wave functions.

Our main results are as follows. Because the translations of p​4​m​mp4mm are not commutators, a chiral state may combine a translation with time reversal, and staggered chiral classes appear, which are absent for p​6​m​mp6mm [74]. Only one of the eight classes, with unitary rotations and mirrors combined with time reversal, admits a Chern number (Secs. III.4 and VI.2). The scalar chirality of every cuboc and conical order alternates under a translation or the fourfold rotation, so a liquid that keeps the magnetic group of such an order has no Chern number and no spontaneous thermal Hall response (Sec. IX.2). This selection rule needs only the magnetic group, but it assumes that the liquid inherits that group, which for cuboc1 is the nematic group p​2​m​mp2mm, whose PSGs we classify separately (Sec. IX.3). Uniformly chiral orders, from which a Chern state could be inherited, exist among the regular orders, but those we find need ferromagnetic bow-tie couplings and sizable further-neighbor couplings (Sec. IX.2), and the regular orders of two phases of Ref. [26] give way to long-wavelength modulations when J×≠0J_{\times}\neq 0 (Sec. IX.1). Unprojected self-consistent mean-field theory selects the uniform class-ℬ\mathcal{B} chiral state, a gapped Chern state (Secs. VI.3 and IX.4), but projection reverses this ranking, as at the nearest-neighbor point [4]. Among the projected wave functions we compare (Sec. IX.5), the cuboc1-ordered state is lowest for strong cross-octagon couplings, a pinwheel valence-bond crystal for weaker ones, and nonchiral states close to decoupled squares and chains near the boundary of the cuboc1 phase. No chiral state, including the nematic chiral state that would inherit the symmetry of cuboc1, is lowest at any coupling considered. This differs from the kagome lattice [9, 8, 39, 27]. Beyond the chiral question, the two site orbits, both with nontrivial site symmetry, reduce the cohomology classes to a much smaller set of algebraic PSGs (Sec. IV). A relative time-reversal sign ζ\zeta between the orbits decides realizability and, for ζ=−\zeta=-, pins sublattice-imbalance flat bands [109, 53] to the Fermi level for any amplitudes (Secs. IV.2 and IV.3). Because the nearest-neighbor graph contains triangles, nearest-neighbor ansätze can already break time reversal (Sec. VI).

Spin–orbit coupling allows spin-dependent spinon hopping whose Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya (DM)-like vectors follow Moriya’s rules relative to the singlet hopping in every PSG, and projective signs invert them only on bonds that carry no singlet hopping (Sec. VIII.1). It turns U⁡(1)U(1) states into mean-field spinon quantum spin Hall insulators (Sec. VIII.2). With conserved SzS^{z} a charge-conjugation theorem confines them to the classes in which no symmetry conjugates the spinon charge, and with generic spin–orbit coupling they also occur in time-reversal-symmetric (TRS) PSGs whose translations conjugate the spinon charge and, rarely, in other particle–hole classes. These states are not stable spin liquids: with conserved SzS^{z} the physical state orders, and with generic spin–orbit coupling the gauge field confines. This fermionic analysis complements a Schwinger-boson study of the effect of ab initio DM interactions on decorated square-kagome magnets [110].

The paper is organized as follows. Section II introduces the lattice and its symmetries, and Sec. III the parton construction and the working definitions. Section IV classifies the projective symmetry groups and derives the flat bands. Sections V and VI construct the symmetric and chiral spin liquids, and Sec. VII discusses their spectra. Section VIII adds spin–orbit coupling. Section IX relates the spin liquids to the noncoplanar orders through classical, self-consistent mean-field, and projected variational calculations, and Sec. X discusses the stability of the mean-field states and a Lieb–Schultz–Mattis-type constraint. Section XI summarizes the results and their limitations. Conventions and derivations are given in the appendices, and method and survey details and all tabulated data in the Supplemental Material (SM) [86].

II Lattice, Symmetries, and Bonds

The square-kagome lattice consists of squares joined at their corners by pairs of triangles, the bow-ties, so that every site is shared by two triangles. Each unit cell contains six sites, twelve nearest-neighbor bonds, four triangles, one square, and one octagon, and every site has four neighbors. Four sites of a cell belong to its square (square sites) and two join neighboring squares (bow-tie sites). We use the ideal geometry, in which all nearest-neighbor bonds have unit length, the triangles are equilateral, and the squares are parallel to the Bravais vectors, the geometry of Fig. 1 of Ref. [26]. With the origin at a square center, the Bravais lattice is spanned by

𝑻1=(a,0),𝑻2=(0,a),a=1+3,\bm{T}_{1}=(a,0),\qquad\bm{T}_{2}=(0,a),\qquad a=1+\sqrt{3}, (1)

and a site is labeled by i=(x,y,μ)i=(x,y,\mu), with 𝒓i=x​𝑻1+y​𝑻2+𝒅μ\bm{r}_{i}=x\bm{T}_{1}+y\bm{T}_{2}+\bm{d}_{\mu} and

𝒅1\displaystyle\bm{d}_{1} =(12,12),\displaystyle=\left(\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{1}{2}\right), 𝒅2\displaystyle\bm{d}_{2} =(−12,12),\displaystyle=\left(-\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{1}{2}\right), 𝒅3\displaystyle\bm{d}_{3} =(−12,−12),\displaystyle=\left(-\tfrac{1}{2},-\tfrac{1}{2}\right),
𝒅4\displaystyle\bm{d}_{4} =(12,−12),\displaystyle=\left(\tfrac{1}{2},-\tfrac{1}{2}\right), 𝒅5\displaystyle\bm{d}_{5} =(a2,0),\displaystyle=\left(\tfrac{a}{2},0\right), 𝒅6\displaystyle\bm{d}_{6} =(0,a2).\displaystyle=\left(0,\tfrac{a}{2}\right). (2)

The square sites μ=1,…,4\mu=1,\dots,4 are numbered counterclockwise, and μ=5\mu=5, 66 are the bow-tie sites between the square at the origin and its neighbors along 𝑻1\bm{T}_{1} and 𝑻2\bm{T}_{2} (Fig. 1). Every triangle has one square edge and two bow-tie edges, so that the nearest-neighbor graph is not bipartite.

The full isometry group of the ideal lattice is the symmorphic wallpaper group p​4​m​mp4mm (see also Ref. [43]), generated by the translations T1T_{1}, T2T_{2}, the rotation C4C_{4} by π/2\pi/2 about the square center at the origin, and the diagonal mirror σ:(X,Y)→(Y,X)\sigma:(X,Y)\to(Y,X). The bow-tie sites occupy the Wyckoff position 2​c2c with site symmetry 2​m​m2mm, and the square sites the position 4​d4d, (±x,±x)(\pm x,\pm x) with x=(3−1)/4x=(\sqrt{3}-1)/4 in units of aa, with site symmetry ..m..m. The generators act on the site labels as
