with words read from right to left. Every site has a nontrivial stabilizer: the bow-tie site (0,0,5)(0,0,5) is fixed by the twofold rotation T1​C42T_{1}C_{4}^{2} about it, by the mirror σ​C4:(X,Y)→(X,−Y)\sigma C_{4}:(X,Y)\to(X,-Y), and by Θ\Theta, which generate ℤ23\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{3}, and the square site (0,0,1)(0,0,1) is fixed by σ\sigma and Θ\Theta, which generate ℤ22\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{2}. These stabilizers, through the on-site representations they must carry, shape the whole classification (Sec. IV).

We include the twelve bond orbits up to the length 1+31+\sqrt{3} of the couplings J×J_{\times} and J+J_{+} across the octagons [26], drawn in Fig. 1(b) and (c). Their lengths, reference bonds, and stabilizers are listed in Sec. SI of the SM. The nearest-neighbor orbits are the square edges J1J_{1} and the bow-tie edges J23J_{23}, whose eight bonds per cell form a single orbit of p​4​m​mp4mm and comprise the couplings J2J_{2} and J3J_{3} of Ref. [26]. At graph distance two lie the square diagonals JdJ_{d} and the orbits Jb​pJ_{bp}, Js​bJ_{sb}, Jb​bJ_{bb}, and Jb​cJ_{bc}, and we call the range that includes them GD2. At graph distance three lie Jo​3J_{o3}, JtJ_{t}, and Jb​sJ_{bs}, and at graph distance four J×J_{\times} and J+J_{+}. The bonds J23J_{23}, Js​bJ_{sb}, and Jo​3J_{o3} join a square site to a bow-tie site, and all other orbits join two sites of the same orbit. This distinction controls the time-reversal selection rules of Sec. IV.2. The mirror σ\sigma fixes the reference bonds of JdJ_{d} and J×J_{\times} with both endpoints, and axial mirrors fix those of Jb​sJ_{bs} and J+J_{+}. These elements constrain the reference amplitudes in addition to the bond-reversing elements. Inequivalent bow-tie edges, as in the J1J_{1}-J2J_{2}-J3J_{3} model of Refs. [23, 26], lower the symmetry to p​4p4, which we do not treat here.

III Parton Mean-Field Theory and Projective Symmetry Groups

III.1 Abrikosov Fermions and Mean-Field Ansätze

We use the standard fermionic parton construction [1, 6, 2, 116] in the conventions of Ref. [59], summarized in Appendix A. The spin is written as 𝑺i=12​fi​α†​𝝈α​β​fi​β\bm{S}_{i}=\frac{1}{2}f^{\dagger}_{i\alpha}\bm{\sigma}_{\alpha\beta}f_{i\beta} with the constraint fi​α†​fi​α=1f^{\dagger}_{i\alpha}f_{i\alpha}=1, and the fermions of site ii form the matrix

ψi=(fi↑fi↓†fi↓−fi↑†),\psi_{i}=\begin{pmatrix}f_{i\uparrow}&f^{\dagger}_{i\downarrow}\\ f_{i\downarrow}&-f^{\dagger}_{i\uparrow}\end{pmatrix}, (5)

on which spin rotations act from the left and S​U​(2)SU(2) gauge transformations from the right, ψi→ψi​Wi†\psi_{i}\to\psi_{i}W_{i}^{\dagger}. Pauli matrices σa\sigma^{a} act in spin space and τa\tau^{a} in gauge space. The mean-field Hamiltonian is

HMF=∑i,j∑α=0,x,y,zTr⁡[σα​ψi​ui​j(α)​ψj†]+∑iTr⁡[ψi​ai​ψi†],H_{\rm MF}=\sum_{i,j}\sum_{\alpha=0,x,y,z}\mathrm{Tr}\left[\sigma^{\alpha}\psi_{i}u^{(\alpha)}_{ij}\psi_{j}^{\dagger}\right]+\sum_{i}\mathrm{Tr}\left[\psi_{i}a_{i}\psi_{i}^{\dagger}\right], (6)

summed over ordered pairs, with the singlet link ui​j(0)u^{(0)}_{ij} and the triplet links ui​j(a)u^{(a)}_{ij},

ui​j(0)\displaystyle u^{(0)}_{ij} =i​χi​j0​τ0+χi​j3​τ3+Δi​j1​τ1+Δi​j2​τ2,\displaystyle=\mathrm{i}\chi^{0}_{ij}\tau^{0}+\chi^{3}_{ij}\tau^{3}+\Delta^{1}_{ij}\tau^{1}+\Delta^{2}_{ij}\tau^{2},
ui​j(a)\displaystyle u^{(a)}_{ij} =ti​ja​0​τ0+i⁡(ti​ja​1​τ1+ti​ja​2​τ2+ti​ja​3​τ3),\displaystyle=t^{a0}_{ij}\tau^{0}+\mathrm{i}\left(t^{a1}_{ij}\tau^{1}+t^{a2}_{ij}\tau^{2}+t^{a3}_{ij}\tau^{3}\right), (7)

real coefficients, and u(α)j​i=u(α)†i​ju^{(\alpha)}_{ji}=u^{(\alpha)\dagger}_{ij}. Here χ0\chi^{0} and χ3\chi^{3} give the spin-independent hopping, Δ1,2\Delta^{1,2} the singlet pairing, and the triplet coefficients spin-dependent hopping and pairing, while the multipliers ai=aik​τka_{i}=a^{k}_{i}\tau^{k} impose the constraint on average. Triplet links are allowed when spin–orbit coupling locks spin rotations to lattice operations, and describe at mean-field level the effect of Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya and other anisotropic exchange [20, 77, 17, 59]. A gauge transformation acts as

ui​j(α)→Wi​ui​j(α)​Wj†,ai→Wi​ai​Wi†,u^{(\alpha)}_{ij}\to W_{i}\,u^{(\alpha)}_{ij}W_{j}^{\dagger},\qquad a_{i}\to W_{i}\,a_{i}W_{i}^{\dagger}, (8)

and gauge-related ansätze describe the same projected state.

III.2 Projective Symmetry and Invariant Gauge Group

A lattice operation OO maps an ansatz ui​ju_{ij} onto uO⁡(i)​O​(j)u_{O(i)O(j)}. Since gauge-related ansätze describe the same spin state, the ansatz is symmetric under OO if the two agree up to a gauge transformation GO​(i)G_{O}(i) [116],

uO⁡(i)​O​(j)(0)\displaystyle u^{(0)}_{O(i)O(j)} =GO​(O⁡(i))​ui​j(0)​GO†​(O⁡(j)),\displaystyle=G_{O}(O(i))\,u^{(0)}_{ij}\,G_{O}^{\dagger}(O(j)),
uO⁡(i)​O​(j)(b)\displaystyle u^{(b)}_{O(i)O(j)} =∑a[RO]b​a​GO​(O⁡(i))​ui​j(a)​GO†​(O⁡(j)),\displaystyle=\sum_{a}\left[R_{O}\right]_{ba}G_{O}(O(i))\,u^{(a)}_{ij}\,G_{O}^{\dagger}(O(j)), (9)

with aO⁡(i)=GO​(O⁡(i))​ai​GO†​(O⁡(i))a_{O(i)}=G_{O}(O(i))\,a_{i}\,G_{O}^{\dagger}(O(i)). Here RO∈S​O​(3)R_{O}\in SO(3) is the spin rotation that accompanies OO in the presence of spin–orbit coupling (Appendix A.2), and without it only the singlet links occur. Time reversal reverses every link and multiplier [116],

ui​j(α)=−GΘ​(i)​ui​j(α)​GΘ†​(j),ai=−GΘ​(i)​ai​GΘ†​(i).u^{(\alpha)}_{ij}=-G_{\Theta}(i)\,u^{(\alpha)}_{ij}\,G_{\Theta}^{\dagger}(j),\qquad a_{i}=-G_{\Theta}(i)\,a_{i}\,G_{\Theta}^{\dagger}(i). (10)

The combined operations GO​OG_{O}O form the projective symmetry group (PSG) of the ansatz. Ansätze with gauge-inequivalent PSGs describe distinct spin liquids, so the PSG plays for a spin liquid the role that the space group plays for a crystal.

The PSG elements that belong to the identity operation, ui​j=G⁡(i)​ui​j​G†​(j)u_{ij}=G(i)\,u_{ij}\,G^{\dagger}(j), form a special subgroup, the invariant gauge group (IGG). It always contains {±τ0}≅ℤ2\{\pm\tau^{0}\}\cong\mathbb{Z}_{2} and fixes the low-energy gauge theory [116]. In the canonical gauge the IGG is global. An ansatz with only imaginary hopping, ui​j(0)=i​χi​j0​τ0u^{(0)}_{ij}=\mathrm{i}\chi^{0}_{ij}\tau^{0} and ai=0a_{i}=0, has the IGG S​U​(2)SU(2), real hopping χi​j3​τ3\chi^{3}_{ij}\tau^{3} lowers it to U⁡(1)={ei​θ​τ3}U(1)=\{e^{\mathrm{i}\theta\tau^{3}}\}, and pairing lowers it to ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}.

PSG elements compose as

GO1​O2​(i)=GO1​(i)​GO2​(O1−1​(i)),G_{O_{1}O_{2}}(i)=G_{O_{1}}(i)\,G_{O_{2}}\big(O_{1}^{-1}(i)\big), (11)

so that every relation (4), which equals the identity for the spins, becomes an element of the IGG for the spinons. The algebraic PSGs are the solutions of these conditions, up to gauge transformations GO​(i)→Wi​GO​(i)​WO−1​(i)†G_{O}(i)\to W_{i}G_{O}(i)W^{\dagger}_{O^{-1}(i)} that preserve the IGG and up to re-liftings, which multiply a generator by an element of the IGG. Because RO∈S​O​(3)R_{O}\in SO(3), the classification is the same with and without spin–orbit coupling. Formulations with S​U​(2)SU(2) spin rotations, as in Ref. [89], carry in addition the double-cover signs, for instance UC44=−1U_{C_{4}}^{4}=-1. Since −1-1 in spin space acts on the spinons as −τ0∈IGG-\tau^{0}\in\mathrm{IGG}, their labels differ from ours by these fixed signs and describe the same PSGs.

On the square-kagome lattice one further condition enters. An element hh of the stabilizer of a site ii maps the site onto itself, so Gh​(i)G_{h}(i) is an on-site S​U​(2)SU(2) matrix, and these matrices must form a representation of the stabilizer that is compatible with the relation values. A PSG is therefore a set of relation values together with an on-site representation for each site orbit. On a lattice whose sites lie at the general position this condition is always met. Here it removes most cohomology classes and splits others (Sec. IV).

III.3 Gauge-Invariant Fluxes

Gauge-inequivalent ansätze are distinguished by their fluxes. For a closed loop CC starting and ending at a base site ii, the flux operator built from the singlet links is [116]

PC(i)=ui​juj​k⋯ul​i.P_{C}(i)=u_{ij}u_{jk}\cdots u_{li}. (12)

A gauge transformation changes it only by a rotation at the base site, PC​(i)→Wi​PC​(i)​Wi†P_{C}(i)\to W_{i}P_{C}(i)W_{i}^{\dagger}. For a loop of length LL it takes the form PC=iL​QCP_{C}=\mathrm{i}^{L}Q_{C} with QC∝cosϕCτ0+isinϕC𝒏^C⋅𝝉Q_{C}\propto\cos\phi_{C}\,\tau^{0}+\mathrm{i}\sin\phi_{C}\,\hat{\bm{n}}_{C}\cdot\bm{\tau}. For hopping ansätze in the canonical gauge, 𝒏^C=𝒛^\hat{\bm{n}}_{C}=\hat{\bm{z}}, and ϕC=L​π/2−ΦC\phi_{C}=L\pi/2-\Phi_{C} (mod 2​π2\pi), where ΦC=arg(ti​jtj​k⋯tl​i)\Phi_{C}=\arg(t_{ij}t_{jk}\cdots t_{li}) is the hopping flux and ti​jt_{ij} is the coefficient of fi​α†​fj​αf^{\dagger}_{i\alpha}f_{j\alpha}. The fluxes also reveal the IGG, which consists of the S​U​(2)SU(2) matrices that commute with all flux operators and on-site terms at the base site. It is S​U​(2)SU(2) if all PC∝τ0P_{C}\propto\tau^{0}, U⁡(1)U(1) if all 𝒏^C\hat{\bm{n}}_{C} are collinear, and ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} otherwise.

With nearest-neighbor bonds, all loops are generated by the faces of the lattice: the four triangles of a cell, the square, and the octagon [Fig. 2(a)–(c)]. Further-neighbor bonds add the triangles of Fig. 2(d)–(f). For U⁡(1)U(1) and S​U​(2)SU(2) ansätze, the counterclockwise hopping fluxes through the faces of a unit cell add up to the flux per cell,

∑△Φ△+Φs+Φo=Φ(mod2​π),\sum_{\triangle}\Phi_{\triangle}+\Phi_{s}+\Phi_{o}=\Phi\pmod{2\pi}, (13)

where Φs\Phi_{s} and Φo\Phi_{o} are the square and octagon fluxes. The PSG fixes Φ\Phi: it is 00 or π\pi for η12=±1\eta_{12}=\pm 1, and continuous in the flux families of Sec. IV.5. In the staggered gauge sectors (wT=1w_{T}=1) the translations conjugate the U⁡(1)U(1) charge, so the face fluxes alternate in sign between neighboring cells and Eq. (13) holds with the sign (−1)x+y(-1)^{x+y}.

Time reversal acts on the flux operators as PC​(i)→(−1)L​GΘ​(i)​PC​(i)​GΘ†​(i)P_{C}(i)\to(-1)^{L}G_{\Theta}(i)P_{C}(i)G_{\Theta}^{\dagger}(i), so loops of odd length are the ones that detect it. In a TRS ansatz, every odd loop has a traceless PCP_{C}, that is, a hopping flux 00 or π\pi. In an S​U​(2)SU(2) ansatz, by contrast, every PC∝τ0P_{C}\propto\tau^{0}, so an odd loop carries the flux ±π/2\pm\pi/2, which is odd under time reversal. A TRS S​U​(2)SU(2) state therefore has no odd loop. Every triangle of the lattice has one square edge and two bow-tie edges, so such a state cannot have amplitudes on both nearest-neighbor orbits.

III.4 Chiral Projective Symmetry Groups

A chiral spin liquid breaks time reversal, but in a restricted way: every lattice symmetry gg is kept, either on its own or combined with time reversal as g​Θg\Theta [47, 115, 8]. We record this choice by a sign ϵ⁡(g)=±1\epsilon(g)=\pm 1, with ϵ⁡(g)=+1\epsilon(g)=+1 if gg is kept on its own and ϵ⁡(g)=−1\epsilon(g)=-1 if only g​Θg\Theta is a symmetry. Since products of symmetries must behave consistently, ϵ⁡(g1​g2)=ϵ⁡(g1)​ϵ​(g2)\epsilon(g_{1}g_{2})=\epsilon(g_{1})\epsilon(g_{2}), so ϵ\epsilon is a character of p​4​m​mp4mm. It is therefore fixed by its values on the generators, which must respect the relations (4).

These relations impose only one condition. Because C4C_{4} turns T1T_{1} into T2T_{2}, the two translations must carry the same sign, ϵ⁡(T1)=ϵ⁡(T2)≡ϵT\epsilon(T_{1})=\epsilon(T_{2})\equiv\epsilon_{T}. The signs ϵT\epsilon_{T}, ϵ⁡(C4)\epsilon(C_{4}), and ϵ⁡(σ)\epsilon(\sigma) are otherwise free, which gives the eight chiral classes of Table 1. In four of them, ϵT=−1\epsilon_{T}=-1: a translation is a symmetry only together with time reversal, so time-reversal-odd quantities, such as the scalar chirality, change sign from one unit cell to the next. We call these classes staggered and mark them with a prime. They exist on every lattice with the symmetry p​4​m​mp4mm (or p​4p4) [74]. They do not exist for p​6​m​mp6mm, where every translation can be written as a product of rotations and therefore always has ϵ=+1\epsilon=+1, nor for p​4​gp4g, where every translation is the square of a glide reflection.

Class ℬ\mathcal{B} is the analog of the Kalmeyer–Laughlin state: translations and rotations are kept, and the mirrors are kept only together with time reversal. As we show in Sec. VI.2, it is the only class that allows a Chern number.

The PSGs of a chiral class are easy to obtain. The symmetries of each class, some of them combined with Θ\Theta, form a group with the same multiplication rules as p​4​m​mp4mm itself. The gauge matrices GgG_{g} therefore satisfy the same equations, and the algebraic PSGs of every chiral class are those of the space group p​4​m​mp4mm alone (Sec. IV.6). The class enters only when an ansatz is built: for an element with ϵ⁡(g)=−1\epsilon(g)=-1, the symmetry condition (9) acquires the extra minus sign of time reversal [8],

ug⁡(i)​g​(j)(α)=−Gg​Θ​(g⁡(i))​[Rg​ui​j](α)​Gg​Θ†​(g⁡(j)).u^{(\alpha)}_{g(i)g(j)}=-\,G_{g\Theta}(g(i))\,\big[R_{g}\,u_{ij}\big]^{(\alpha)}\,G^{\dagger}_{g\Theta}(g(j)). (14)

III.5 Working Definitions and Units

Realized PSG. An ansatz built from a PSG can accidentally be invariant under a larger gauge group, and it then belongs to a different PSG. We call a PSG realized at a given range if a generic ansatz with all amplitudes it allows up to that range has exactly the IGG of the PSG, and a connected bond graph. A chiral PSG must, in addition, break time reversal.

Other terms. A state descends from a parent if its PSG is a subgroup of the parent PSG and it has a smaller IGG. A descendant is genuine if it is realized with bonds up to J+J_{+}. The bow-tie sites and the square sites form the two site orbits, and symmetry-related bonds form bond orbits, named by their couplings. The extended stabilizer of a site is its stabilizer in p​4​m​m×ℤ2Θp4mm\times\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{\Theta}, extended by the IGG. A sector of U⁡(1)U(1) PSGs collects the PSGs in which the same symmetries reverse the U⁡(1)U(1) rotation (Sec. IV.5).

Sampled results. Spectral types, Dirac flavor numbers, and the Chern numbers of our surveys are computed at fixed amplitudes. They describe regions of amplitude space, not the PSG as a whole. Only the flat bands (Sec. IV.3) and the symmetry selection rules hold for all amplitudes.

Units. Spinon energies are given in units of the hopping |t||t| on a reference bond, with ti​j=2​(i​χi​j0−χi​j3)t_{ij}=2(\mathrm{i}\chi^{0}_{ij}-\chi^{3}_{ij}) the coefficient of fi​α†​fj​αf^{\dagger}_{i\alpha}f_{j\alpha}. Energies of Heisenberg models are per site, in units of |J1||J_{1}|, for S=1/2S=1/2. The gap Δ\Delta is the single-spinon gap, in units of |t||t| for free amplitudes and of |J1||J_{1}| for the self-consistent states of Sec. IX.4. The two-spinon continuum starts at 2​Δ2\Delta.

IV Algebraic PSGs

We now solve the PSGs [the derivations are outlined in Appendix B]. For the IGG ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}, a PSG is fixed by two pieces of data. The first is its set of relation values, one sign ±1\pm 1 for each relation (4). Gauge-inequivalent sets of signs are classified by the cohomology group H2​(p​4​m​m×ℤ2Θ,ℤ2)=ℤ210H^{2}(p4mm\times\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{\Theta},\mathbb{Z}_{2})=\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{10}, so there are 210=10242^{10}=1024 classes. The second is how the symmetries that leave a site fixed act on that site. These elements form the site stabilizer, and their gauge matrices Gh​(i)G_{h}(i) are on-site S​U​(2)SU(2) matrices that must be consistent with the relation values.

On a lattice whose sites have no symmetry of their own, the second condition is always satisfied, and every class gives exactly one PSG. On the square-kagome lattice both site orbits have nontrivial stabilizers. A class can therefore give no PSG, if one of the orbits admits no consistent on-site matrices, or more than one, if the two orbits admit several inequivalent combinations [66, 10].

IV.1 ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} Projective Symmetry Groups

In a suitable gauge, every ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} PSG of the square-kagome lattice takes the form

GT1​(x,y,μ)\displaystyle G_{T_{1}}(x,y,\mu) =τ0,\displaystyle=\tau^{0},
GT2​(x,y,μ)\displaystyle G_{T_{2}}(x,y,\mu) =η12x​τ0,\displaystyle=\eta_{12}^{x}\,\tau^{0},
GC4​(x,y,μ)\displaystyle G_{C_{4}}(x,y,\mu) =ηC4​Tx​η12x​y​gC4​(μ),\displaystyle=\eta_{C_{4}T}^{\,x}\,\eta_{12}^{\,xy}\,g_{C_{4}}(\mu),
Gσ​(x,y,μ)\displaystyle G_{\sigma}(x,y,\mu) =ησ​Tx+y​η12x​y​gσ​(μ),\displaystyle=\eta_{\sigma T}^{\,x+y}\,\eta_{12}^{\,xy}\,g_{\sigma}(\mu),
GΘ​(x,y,μ)\displaystyle G_{\Theta}(x,y,\mu) =ηΘ​Tx+y​gΘ​(μ).\displaystyle=\eta_{\Theta T}^{\,x+y}\,g_{\Theta}(\mu). (15)

The dependence on the cell (x,y)(x,y) is a set of signs, and the sublattice matrices gO​(μ)g_{O}(\mu) can be chosen from the quaternion group {±τ0,±i​τ1,±i​τ2,±i​τ3}\{\pm\tau^{0},\pm\mathrm{i}\tau^{1},\pm\mathrm{i}\tau^{2},\pm\mathrm{i}\tau^{3}\}, with gC4​(μ)=τ0g_{C_{4}}(\mu)=\tau^{0} for μ=2,3,4,6\mu=2,3,4,6. Restricting to the quaternion group loses nothing: every site stabilizer here is a product of ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} factors, whose S​U​(2)SU(2) representations can always be rotated into this group.

A ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} class is labeled by ten signs, the values of the following relations:

η12:T2​T1​T2−1​T1−1,\displaystyle\eta_{12}:\ T_{2}T_{1}T_{2}^{-1}T_{1}^{-1}, ηΘ​σ:σ​Θ​σ−1​Θ−1,\displaystyle\eta_{\Theta\sigma}:\ \sigma\Theta\sigma^{-1}\Theta^{-1},
ηC4​T:C4​T2​C4−1​T1,\displaystyle\eta_{C_{4}T}:\ C_{4}T_{2}C_{4}^{-1}T_{1}, ηΘ​C4:C4​Θ​C4−1​Θ−1,\displaystyle\eta_{\Theta C_{4}}:\ C_{4}\Theta C_{4}^{-1}\Theta^{-1},
ησ​T:σ​T1​σ−1​T2−1,\displaystyle\eta_{\sigma T}:\ \sigma T_{1}\sigma^{-1}T_{2}^{-1}, ησ:σ2,ησ​C4:(σ​C4)2,\displaystyle\eta_{\sigma}:\ \sigma^{2},\quad\eta_{\sigma C_{4}}:\ (\sigma C_{4})^{2},
ηΘ​T:T1​Θ​T1−1​Θ−1,\displaystyle\eta_{\Theta T}:\ T_{1}\Theta T_{1}^{-1}\Theta^{-1}, ηC4:C44,ηΘ:Θ2.\displaystyle\eta_{C_{4}}:\ C_{4}^{4},\quad\eta_{\Theta}:\ \Theta^{2}. (16)

The other relations add nothing new. We set C4​T1​C4−1​T2−1=+1C_{4}T_{1}C_{4}^{-1}T_{2}^{-1}=+1 by multiplying GT1G_{T_{1}} by −1-1 if needed, and the relations for T2T_{2} repeat ησ​T\eta_{\sigma T} and ηΘ​T\eta_{\Theta T}. Six of the ten signs belong to the space group, three tell whether time reversal commutes with T1T_{1}, σ\sigma, and C4C_{4}, and one is ηΘ\eta_{\Theta}.

Three signs have no counterpart on lattices with p​6​m​mp6mm symmetry, such as the kagome lattice. With ηC4​T=−1\eta_{C_{4}T}=-1 or ησ​T=−1\eta_{\sigma T}=-1, the rotation or the mirror commutes with the translations only up to a sign. With ηΘ​T=−1\eta_{\Theta T}=-1, time reversal carries the alternating sign (−1)x+y(-1)^{x+y} on the spinons.

We label a ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} PSG by these signs, Z​nT2​nC4​T​nσ​T\mathrm{Z}n_{T_{2}}n_{C_{4}T}n_{\sigma T}-nΘ​T​nΘ​σ​nΘ​C4n_{\Theta T}n_{\Theta\sigma}n_{\Theta C_{4}}-nσ​nσ​C4​nC4​(nΘ)n_{\sigma}n_{\sigma C_{4}}n_{C_{4}}(n_{\Theta}), with the digit 00 for +1+1 and 11 for −1-1, for example Z000-011-100(1). Here nT2n_{T_{2}} stands for η12\eta_{12}. A sign ζ=±\zeta=\pm is appended when a class has two PSGs (Sec. IV.2). The sublattice matrices of all PSGs are given in the SM.

The on-site condition reduces the 10241024 classes to 200200 PSGs. Consistent on-site matrices exist on the bow-tie sites, with stabilizer 2​m​m×ℤ2Θ≅ℤ232mm\times\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{\Theta}\cong\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{3}, for 240240 classes, and on the square sites, with stabilizer m×ℤ2Θ≅ℤ22m\times\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{\Theta}\cong\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{2}, for 640640. Only the 160160 classes allowed on both orbits survive. Of these, 120120 give one PSG and 4040 give two, for a total of 120+2×40=200120+2\times 40=200 ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} PSGs (Appendix B and Sec. SII of the SM). A script in the data files [86] checks the classification independently: it reconstructs every PSG from its canonical form, evaluates all group relations, distinguishes the 200200 ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} PSGs by gauge invariants, and recomputes the realized PSGs of Sec. V. The two orbits alone form a checkerboard lattice and a lattice of squares. How their PSGs combine into those of the square-kagome lattice, and the counts for other p​4​m​mp4mm lattices, are given in Sec. SIII of the SM.

IV.2 The Relative Time-Reversal Sign

The 4040 classes with two PSGs are those in which time reversal acts on every site as a plain sign, GΘ=hb​τ0G_{\Theta}=h_{b}\tau^{0} on the bow-tie sites and GΘ=hs​τ0G_{\Theta}=h_{s}\tau^{0} on the square sites. All four time-reversal signs of these classes, ηΘ\eta_{\Theta}, ηΘ​T\eta_{\Theta T}, ηΘ​σ\eta_{\Theta\sigma}, and ηΘ​C4\eta_{\Theta C_{4}}, are +1+1. The two PSGs of such a class differ only in the relative sign

ζ=hb​hs=14​Tr​GΘ​(0,0,5)​Tr​GΘ​(0,0,1),\zeta=h_{b}h_{s}=\tfrac{1}{4}\mathrm{Tr}G_{\Theta}(0,0,5)\,\mathrm{Tr}G_{\Theta}(0,0,1), (17)

which no gauge transformation can change.

This sign decides which bonds are allowed. With GΘ​(i)=hi​τ0G_{\Theta}(i)=h_{i}\tau^{0}, the time-reversal condition (10) becomes ui​j=−hi​hj​ui​ju_{ij}=-h_{i}h_{j}\,u_{ij} and ai=−aia_{i}=-a_{i}. On-site terms therefore always vanish, and a bond survives only if hi​hj=−1h_{i}h_{j}=-1:

  • •

    For ζ=+\zeta=+, all hih_{i} are equal, and every amplitude vanishes, on every bond at any range. These PSGs describe no state at all.

  • •

    For ζ=−\zeta=-, bonds within a site orbit vanish, and only the bonds between square and bow-tie sites survive (J23J_{23}, Js​bJ_{sb}, and Jo​3J_{o3} up to J+J_{+}).

The same holds for U⁡(1)U(1) and S​U​(2)SU(2) PSGs in which time reversal acts as a sign. The PSGs with no amplitude are exactly the ζ=+\zeta=+ ones: 4040 ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}, 2525 U⁡(1)U(1), and 44 S​U​(2)SU(2) PSGs. Every other PSG is realized by bonds up to J+J_{+} (Sec. V).

IV.3 Flat Bands at the Fermi Level

The sign ζ\zeta has a direct effect on the spinon bands. In a PSG with ζ=−\zeta=-, only bonds between square and bow-tie sites survive (Sec. IV.2), for singlet and triplet amplitudes alike. The Bloch Hamiltonian therefore connects only the two site orbits,

h⁡(𝒌)=(0B⁡(𝒌)B†​(𝒌)0),h(\bm{k})=\begin{pmatrix}0&B(\bm{k})\\ B^{\dagger}(\bm{k})&0\end{pmatrix}, (18)

where B⁡(𝒌)B(\bm{k}) is a 4×24\times 2 matrix between the four square sites and the two bow-tie sites of a cell, per spin (8×48\times 4 in Nambu space). A 4×24\times 2 matrix has rank at most two, so h⁡(𝒌)h(\bm{k}) has at least two zero modes per spin at every momentum. These modes form exactly flat bands at E=0E=0. At half filling they are half filled and pinned to the Fermi level, for any amplitudes on J23J_{23}, Js​bJ_{sb}, and Jo​3J_{o3}.

These are the familiar zero modes of a bipartite hopping problem with unequal sublattices [109, 53]. The new element is that here they are imposed by the projective action of time reversal, not by the lattice geometry. The same mechanism works on any lattice with two site orbits of unequal size that admits a PSG with ζ=−\zeta=-. On the square-kagome lattice this covers 4040 ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}, 2525 U⁡(1)U(1) (including one flux family), and 44 S​U​(2)SU(2) PSGs. Only for these PSGs are the bands flat for all amplitudes. The flat bands carry an extensive degeneracy at half filling, which interactions, gauge fluctuations, or the projection will lift, and we do not study their fate here.

IV.4 S​U​(2)SU(2) Projective Symmetry Groups

An S​U​(2)SU(2) ansatz has only imaginary hopping, ui​j(0)=i​χi​j​τ0u^{(0)}_{ij}=\mathrm{i}\chi_{ij}\tau^{0}, and its IGG contains every uniform S​U​(2)SU(2) matrix. Any uniform part of a gauge matrix GO​(i)G_{O}(i) can therefore be absorbed into the IGG, and only a site-dependent sign is left. An S​U​(2)SU(2) PSG is thus a pattern of signs on the lattice: a ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} PSG in which all on-site matrices are ±τ0\pm\tau^{0}. The sign ηΘ\eta_{\Theta} no longer distinguishes PSGs, since it can be absorbed in the same way. We find 88 S​U​(2)SU(2) PSGs, four classes each with ζ=±\zeta=\pm,

SU​000​-​000​-​000±,SU​011​-​000​-​001±,SU​100​-​000​-​000±,SU​111​-​000​-​001±,\begin{gathered}\mathrm{SU}000\text{-}000\text{-}000\pm,\quad\mathrm{SU}011\text{-}000\text{-}001\pm,\\ \mathrm{SU}100\text{-}000\text{-}000\pm,\quad\mathrm{SU}111\text{-}000\text{-}001\pm,\end{gathered} (19)

labeled like the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} PSGs without the digit nΘn_{\Theta}. Only the four PSGs with ζ=−\zeta=- give states, all with bonds between square and bow-tie sites only.

IV.5 U⁡(1)U(1) Projective Symmetry Groups

For the IGG U⁡(1)={ei​θ​τ3}U(1)=\{e^{\mathrm{i}\theta\tau^{3}}\}, every gauge matrix either keeps or reverses the U⁡(1)U(1) rotation,

GO​(i)=ei​ϕO​(i)​τ3​(i​τ1)wO,G_{O}(i)=e^{\mathrm{i}\phi_{O}(i)\tau^{3}}(\mathrm{i}\tau^{1})^{w_{O}}, (20)

with wO=0w_{O}=0 if OO keeps it and wO=1w_{O}=1 if OO reverses it, that is, if OO exchanges spinon particles and holes. As for the chiral classes, C4C_{4} forces wT1=wT2≡wTw_{T_{1}}=w_{T_{2}}\equiv w_{T}, but nothing forces wT=0w_{T}=0. The choices w=(wT,wC4,wσ,wΘ)w=(w_{T},w_{C_{4}},w_{\sigma},w_{\Theta}) give 1616 sectors, twice as many as for p​6​m​mp6mm. In the eight staggered sectors, wT=1w_{T}=1, the translations exchange spinon particles and holes. These sectors still describe TRS states. They should not be confused with the staggered chiral classes of Sec. III.4, in which a translation is combined with time reversal.

Table 2 gives three counts for each sector, which follow the same steps as for ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}. The first column counts all cohomology classes, 18561856 in total. The on-site conditions on the two site orbits keep 5656 of them (second column). As for ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}, some classes then split into two PSGs that differ only in the relative on-site data of the two orbits, which gives 8080 discrete U⁡(1)U(1) PSGs (third column). The sectors with wΘ=0w_{\Theta}=0 contain 4848 discrete PSGs and the two flux families, exactly the 2525 U⁡(1)U(1) PSGs with ζ=+\zeta=+ and the 2525 with ζ=−\zeta=- (Sec. IV.2). Every U⁡(1)U(1) PSG with wΘ=0w_{\Theta}=0 is therefore either empty or a flat-band PSG, and the 3232 U⁡(1)U(1) states with bonds within the site orbits are exactly those with wΘ=1w_{\Theta}=1, the class-AII PSGs of Sec. VIII.2.

One sector is special. In w=(0,0,1,0)w=(0,0,1,0), where only the mirror reverses the U⁡(1)U(1) rotation, the translations need to commute only up to a phase, T2​T1​T2−1​T1−1=ei​Φ​τ3T_{2}T_{1}T_{2}^{-1}T_{1}^{-1}=e^{\mathrm{i}\Phi\tau^{3}}, with any flux Φ∈[0,π]\Phi\in[0,\pi] per unit cell. This gives two continuous families of PSGs. Only the family with ζ=−\zeta=- allows amplitudes, on square–bow-tie bonds only, and its octagon flux varies continuously with Φ\Phi.

We label the discrete U⁡(1)U(1) PSGs Uww-nn, with the sector w=wT​wC4​wσ​wΘw=w_{T}w_{C_{4}}w_{\sigma}w_{\Theta} and an index nn within the sector, and the two families U0010-F0 and U0010-F1. Their forms are given in the SM.

IV.6 The Space Group Alone

Without time reversal we obtain the PSGs of the space group p​4​m​mp4mm alone. These are the PSGs of every chiral class (Sec. III.4): 4040 ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}, 2424 discrete U⁡(1)U(1) PSGs and one flux family, and 44 S​U​(2)SU(2) PSGs (Table 3). Their labels drop the time-reversal digits and ζ\zeta, and carry the chiral class as a prefix, for example ℬ\mathcal{B}:SU011-001.

All PSG labels in this paper follow the same scheme:

  • •

    The letters Z, U, and SU give the IGG.

  • •

    The digits give the relation signs, with 00 for +1+1 and 11 for −1-1. For U⁡(1)U(1) they give the sector ww followed by an index nn.

  • •

    A label without a prefix, such as Z000-011-100(1), is a TRS PSG of p​4​m​m×ℤ2Θp4mm\times\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{\Theta}.

  • •

    A prefix 𝒜\mathcal{A}–𝒟\mathcal{D} or 𝒜′\mathcal{A}^{\prime}–𝒟′\mathcal{D}^{\prime}, such as ℬ\mathcal{B}:SU011-001, gives the chiral class of a time-reversal-breaking PSG.

  • •

    A prefix N, such as N:U1000-0 or N:Z00000-110, marks a PSG of the nematic group of cuboc1 (Sec. IX.3).

Table 4 lists the states that recur in the text.

V Symmetric Spin Liquids

V.1 Construction

To build an ansatz from a PSG, we fix the amplitudes on one reference bond of each bond orbit, and the PSG then gives them on all other bonds of the orbit. The reference amplitudes are restricted by time reversal and by every symmetry that maps the bond onto itself. These are the elements that reverse the bond and, for JdJ_{d}, J×J_{\times}, Jb​sJ_{bs}, and J+J_{+}, also mirrors that fix both of its ends. Equations (9) and (10) then become linear equations for the real coefficients in Eq. (7), and their solutions are the allowed amplitudes. On-site terms are restricted in the same way by the site stabilizers.

For each PSG we then check whether it is realized (Sec. III.5), by computing the IGG of a generic allowed ansatz on a finite patch. Self-consistent multipliers cannot reduce this IGG, since they commute with it.11 1 The mean-field free energy at T>0T>0 is strictly concave in the multipliers and invariant under the IGG of the bonds, so its unique maximum commutes with that IGG. T=0T=0 is reached as the limit T→0+T\to 0^{+}. A realized PSG need not solve the self-consistency equations of a given Hamiltonian, a question we turn to in Sec. IX.

V.2 Realized Spin Liquids

Every PSG except the ζ=+\zeta=+ ones of Sec. IV.2 is realized with bonds up to J+J_{+}. This gives 160160 ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}, 5757 U⁡(1)U(1), and 44 S​U​(2)SU(2) spin liquids, 221221 in total. They fall into two groups:

  • •

    The 6969 states with ζ=−\zeta=- have bonds only between square and bow-tie sites, and the flat bands of Sec. IV.3. They include all four S​U​(2)SU(2) states. Since they forbid the square-edge amplitude, they are not candidates for a model with a dominant J1J_{1}.

  • •

    The other 152152 states, 120120 ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} and 3232 U⁡(1)U(1), also have bonds within the site orbits.

With singlet and triplet amplitudes, all 221221 PSGs are realized already with nearest-neighbor bonds. With singlet amplitudes only, 4040 ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}, 2121 U⁡(1)U(1), and the 44 S​U​(2)SU(2) PSGs are realized with nearest-neighbor bonds, 156156, 5757, and 44 with all orbits at graph distance two, and all 221221 once Jo​3J_{o3} is added. The couplings {J1,J23,J×,J+}\{J_{1},J_{23},J_{\times},J_{+}\} of Ref. [26] realize 6666, 2727, and 44 (Table S3 of the SM).

The triangles of the lattice matter here. On a lattice whose nearest-neighbor bonds form a bipartite graph, a TRS nearest-neighbor ansatz always has a larger IGG when Θ2=−1\Theta^{2}=-1, so such ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} PSGs cannot be realized at that range [85]. The triangles of the square-kagome lattice remove this restriction: 3636 of the 4040 ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} PSGs realized with nearest-neighbor singlets have ηΘ=−1\eta_{\Theta}=-1. The amplitudes and shortest realizing range of every spin liquid are given in the SM.

The realized PSGs are linked by a hierarchy: each S​U​(2)SU(2) state has U⁡(1)U(1) and ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} descendants obtained by adding symmetry-allowed amplitudes. The full map is given in Appendix C.

V.3 Flux States of Ref. [4]

Reference [4] labels its nearest-neighbor states by the hopping fluxes (Φud,Φlr,Φs)(\Phi_{\rm ud},\Phi_{\rm lr},\Phi_{s}) through the up and down triangles, the left and right triangles, and the square. Table 5 gives the PSGs of its eight states, and the four chiral states are discussed in Sec. VI.3. Two remarks help in reading the table. First, (π,0,0)(\pi,0,0) and (π,0,π)(\pi,0,\pi) are fully symmetric even though up/down and left/right triangles carry different fluxes. The reason is that C4C_{4} and the mirror act together with the particle–hole transformation i​τ1\mathrm{i}\tau^{1}, which turns a triangle flux 00 into π\pi and vice versa. Second, changing the sign of all hoppings shifts every triangle flux by π\pi but leaves squares and octagons unchanged, so, for example, (0,0,0)(0,0,0) and (π,π,0)(\pi,\pi,0) are the same state.

Our spectra agree with Ref. [4] for seven of its eight states. The exception is (π,0,π)(\pi,0,\pi), which that work lists with a Fermi surface. We find it gapped, with Δ=3−1\Delta=\sqrt{3}-1 at equal amplitudes and a nonzero gap for all amplitude ratios. Its on-site constraints require a staggered multiplier on the bow-tie sites (Sec. VII.2).

VI Chiral Spin Liquids

VI.1 Realization

On a bipartite lattice, a nearest-neighbor ansatz is always gauge-equivalent to its time-reversed partner. Consequently, realizing a genuinely chiral ansatz requires longer-range bonds. The triangular plaquettes of the square-kagome lattice remove this restriction, allowing chiral ansätze to be realized even with nearest-neighbor bonds. Table 6 summarizes the number of realized chiral PSGs (Sec. III.5) in each class. With singlet amplitudes on all orbits up to J+J_{+}, every chiral PSG of every class is realized. The four S​U​(2)SU(2) PSGs of class 𝒜\mathcal{A} need orbits beyond graph distance two and therefore appear in no column of Table 6. With triplet amplitudes, every chiral PSG is realized already with nearest-neighbor bonds.

The classes ℬ\mathcal{B}, 𝒞\mathcal{C}, ℬ′\mathcal{B}^{\prime}, and 𝒞′\mathcal{C}^{\prime} realize more PSGs with nearest-neighbor bonds because they allow a time-reversal-odd flux through the triangles. Each triangle is mapped onto itself by the mirror through its bow-tie corner, which reverses its orientation and hence its flux. A nonzero flux can survive only if this mirror is combined with time reversal, which reverses the flux once more. This is the case in ℬ\mathcal{B}, 𝒞\mathcal{C}, ℬ′\mathcal{B}^{\prime}, and 𝒞′\mathcal{C}^{\prime}, and not in 𝒜\mathcal{A}, 𝒟\mathcal{D}, 𝒜′\mathcal{A}^{\prime}, and 𝒟′\mathcal{D}^{\prime}. The sign pattern of the flux then follows from the class [Fig. 3(a)–(d)]: uniform in ℬ\mathcal{B}, alternating under C4C_{4} in 𝒞\mathcal{C}, alternating between neighboring cells in ℬ′\mathcal{B}^{\prime}, and both in 𝒞′\mathcal{C}^{\prime}. In general, a symmetry gg maps the flux of a loop PP onto Φ⁡(g​P)=ϵ⁡(g)​det(g)​Φ​(P)\Phi(gP)=\epsilon(g)\det(g)\Phi(P).

VI.2 Chern Numbers and Selection Rule

The same rule applies to the Chern number CC of the occupied spinon bands. A unitary mirror and time reversal each reverse CC, so a symmetry gg maps C→ϵ⁡(g)​det(g)​CC\to\epsilon(g)\det(g)\,C. A nonzero Chern number therefore needs ϵ⁡(g)=det(g)\epsilon(g)=\det(g) for every gg: translations and rotations must be unitary, and mirrors must be combined with time reversal. Among the eight classes, only class ℬ\mathcal{B} satisfies this. In all others, at least one symmetry reverses CC and forces C=0C=0: a translation combined with Θ\Theta in the staggered classes, C4​ΘC_{4}\Theta in 𝒞\mathcal{C}, 𝒟\mathcal{D}, 𝒞′\mathcal{C}^{\prime}, and 𝒟′\mathcal{D}^{\prime}, and a unitary mirror in 𝒜\mathcal{A} and 𝒞\mathcal{C}.

Two rotations will matter later. The twofold rotation C42C_{4}^{2} about the square center is unitary in every class, since it is the square of C4C_{4}. The twofold rotations T1​C42T_{1}C_{4}^{2} and T2​C42T_{2}C_{4}^{2} about the bow-tie sites carry the sign ϵT\epsilon_{T}, so they are combined with Θ\Theta in all staggered classes.

We computed Chern numbers for all realized chiral PSGs at three amplitude points, with the Fukui–Hatsugai–Suzuki method [24]. For ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} states we quote the Kitaev index ν\nu of the Bogoliubov–de Gennes bands, normalized so that ν=−4​C\nu=-4C for a state with Chern number CC per spin. As required, every gapped state outside class ℬ\mathcal{B} has C=0C=0. In class ℬ\mathcal{B} we find C=±1C=\pm 1 and ±2\pm 2 per spin for U⁡(1)U(1) states, C=±1C=\pm 1 for S​U​(2)SU(2) states (all from ℬ\mathcal{B}:SU011-001), and ν=±4\nu=\pm 4 and ±8\pm 8 for ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} states. These values are consistent with the eigenvalues of the fourfold rotation at its fixed momenta, which fix CC modulo 44 [21].

VI.3 Chiral Flux States and the Class-ℬ\mathcal{B} State

The four chiral flux states of Ref. [4] have flux π/2\pi/2 through every triangle. They belong to class ℬ\mathcal{B} if this flux is the same on all triangles, and to class 𝒞\mathcal{C} if it alternates between the up/down and left/right triangles, for either square flux 00 or π\pi (Table 5). Only one of them has a Chern number: ℬ\mathcal{B}:SU011-001, with flux π/2\pi/2 through every triangle and π\pi through squares and octagons [Fig. 3(e)]. We call it the class-ℬ\mathcal{B} state.

At equal amplitudes, the class-ℬ\mathcal{B} state has the single-spinon gap Δ=2−2≈0.586\Delta=2-\sqrt{2}\approx 0.586 and Chern number C=−1C=-1 per spin, and its time-reversed partner has C=+1C=+1. Ribbons along 𝑻1\bm{T}_{1} and 𝑻1+𝑻2\bm{T}_{1}+\bm{T}_{2} carry one chiral edge mode per spin on each edge [Fig. 3(f)], as the Chern number requires. Sign conventions are fixed in Appendix A.1.

The chiral edge modes give a thermal Hall response. For free spinons [108],

κx​yT=−ds3π2∑n∫BZd2​k2​πΩn(𝒌)g2(εn​(𝒌)−μkB​T),\frac{\kappa_{xy}}{T}=-d_{s}\,\frac{3}{\pi^{2}}\sum_{n}\int_{\rm BZ}\frac{d^{2}k}{2\pi}\,\Omega_{n}(\bm{k})\,g_{2}\!\left(\frac{\varepsilon_{n}(\bm{k})-\mu}{k_{B}T}\right), (21)

in units of π​kB2/(6​ℏ)\pi k_{B}^{2}/(6\hbar), where Ωn\Omega_{n} is the Berry curvature of band nn, g2(x)=∫x∞y2(−∂yf)dyg_{2}(x)=\int_{x}^{\infty}y^{2}(-\partial_{y}f)\,dy, and ds=2d_{s}=2 counts the spin species. For kB​T≲0.15​Δk_{B}T\lesssim 0.15\Delta it reaches the plateau −ds​C=+2-d_{s}C=+2 [Fig. 3(g)]. This is a mean-field value. After projection, a gapped state with C=±1C=\pm 1 per spin is expected to become a Kalmeyer-Laughlin spin liquid [47, 115], with chiral central charge c=∓1c=\mp 1, half the free-spinon value, because the gauge field removes one chiral mode. For the state of Fig. 3, with C=−1C=-1, this gives c=+1c=+1. More generally, a U⁡(1)U(1) state with |C|≥2|C|\geq 2 gives |c|=2​|C|−1|c|=2|C|-1, and a ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} state with Kitaev index ν\nu gives c=ν/2c=\nu/2 [50]. A class-ℬ\mathcal{B} ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} state with ν=+4\nu=+4 therefore has c=+2c=+2, whereas an S​U​(2)SU(2) or U⁡(1)U(1) state with the same ν\nu, that is C=−1C=-1, has c=+1c=+1: the two describe different topological orders.

VII Spinon Spectra

We now look at the spinon bands of the realized states, with the mean-field amplitudes treated as free parameters. At half filling a state can be gapped, have Dirac nodes or nodal lines, have Fermi pockets, or, on this lattice, have exactly flat bands at the Fermi level. Except for the flat bands of Sec. IV.3 and nine U⁡(1)U(1) classes with forced zero modes (Sec. VIII.2), the PSG alone does not fix which of these occurs.

Spinon momenta refer to the canonical gauge of Eq. (15). A different choice of gauge shifts them by (π,0)(\pi,0), (0,π)(0,\pi), or (π,π)(\pi,\pi) for ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} states, and by any amount for U⁡(1)U(1) and S​U​(2)SU(2) states, without changing spectral types, gaps, or Chern numbers.

To compare all states on an equal footing, we evaluate each ansatz at a fixed point in its amplitude space, denoted as Point A. At this point, all singlet amplitudes allowed up to J+J_{+} are included, with magnitudes set to 11 (J1J_{1}), 0.90.9 (J23J_{23}), 0.50.5 (JdJ_{d}), 0.450.45 (Jb​pJ_{bp}), 0.40.4 (Js​bJ_{sb}, Jb​bJ_{bb}), 0.350.35 (Jb​cJ_{bc}), 0.30.3 (Jo​3J_{o3}, J×J_{\times}), and 0.250.25 (JtJ_{t}, Jb​sJ_{bs}, J+J_{+}). Their directions are chosen randomly within the corresponding symmetry-allowed spaces, and the Lagrange multipliers are determined self-consistently. Including all symmetry-allowed bonds helps avoid accidental nodal lines that may arise when certain amplitudes are omitted. Point B uses the same amplitude magnitudes but different random directions.

VII.1 Nearest-Neighbor S​U​(2)SU(2) States

The two nearest-neighbor S​U​(2)SU(2) states with bonds on the bow-tie edges have simple closed-form bands. With hopping tbt_{b}, both have two flat bands at E=0E=0. The other bands are

E2=4​tb2±2​tb2​[(1−cos⁡k1)​(1−cos⁡k2)]1/2E^{2}=4t_{b}^{2}\pm 2t_{b}^{2}\left[(1-\cos k_{1})(1-\cos k_{2})\right]^{1/2} (22)

for SU000-000-000−-, which touch the flat bands at MM, and

E2=4tb2±2tb2(1+sink1sink2)1/2E^{2}=4t_{b}^{2}\pm 2t_{b}^{2}\left(1+\sin k_{1}\sin k_{2}\right)^{1/2} (23)

for SU011-000-001−-, which stay at least |tb|​(4−2​2)1/2≈1.08​|tb||t_{b}|(4-2\sqrt{2})^{1/2}\approx 1.08|t_{b}| away from them [Fig. 4(e), (f)]. Here ki=𝒌⋅𝑻ik_{i}=\bm{k}\cdot\bm{T}_{i}.

VII.2 Nearest-Neighbor U⁡(1)U(1) States

Figure 4(a)–(d) shows the band structures of the four TRS flux states listed in Table 5. Two of these states exhibit a flat band for arbitrary ratios of the J1J_{1} and J23J_{23} hopping amplitudes. For the (0,0,0)(0,0,0) state, the flat band occurs at energy ±2​|t1|\pm 2|t_{1}|, where t1t_{1} denotes the hopping amplitude associated with J1J_{1}, consistent with the flat band found in the corresponding tight-binding model [75]. In contrast, for the (π,0,0)(\pi,0,0) state, the flat band lies at the Fermi energy and is entirely localized on the square-lattice sites. Including further-neighbor hopping amplitudes disperses this flat band, giving rise to Fermi pockets. The (0,0,π)(0,0,\pi) state, on the other hand, exhibits two Dirac nodes per spin.

At zero Lagrange multipliers, these states do not satisfy the on-site constraint exactly. For the (0,0,0)(0,0,0) and (0,0,π)(0,0,\pi) states, the square sites accommodate 1.8881.888 and 2.1062.106 fermions per spin per unit cell, respectively, rather than the required value of 22. This imbalance between the two site orbits necessitates distinct Lagrange multipliers for the two orbits. In the gapped (π,0,π)(\pi,0,\pi) state, the two bow-tie sites within a unit cell accommodate 0.330.33 and 0.670.67 fermions per spin, respectively. Enforcing the on-site constraint therefore requires different Lagrange multipliers on these sites, a distinction permitted by the PSG.

VII.3 Spectral Types

Table 7 lists the spectral types of all 221221 realized TRS states at Point A. Apart from the flat-band states, nodal lines are the most common type, and only 1212 states are gapped. The Dirac states have Nf=4N_{f}=4 to 3636 Dirac cones in the Brillouin zone, counting both spin species, for ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} states, and Nf=16N_{f}=16 or 2020 for U⁡(1)U(1) states. The large values come from nodes at general momenta, which the point group copies up to eight times, and from enlarged unit cells. The types are fairly robust. At Point B we rechecked the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} and U⁡(1)U(1) states that are gapped or have point nodes at Point A, together with one ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} state with small nodal loops. Of these, 3434 of the 4343 ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} states and 44 of the 55 U⁡(1)U(1) states keep their type. Amplitudes, spectra, and densities of states of all states are given in the SM.

Outside the ζ=−\zeta=- PSGs, flat bands at the Fermi level need fine-tuned amplitudes. With nearest-neighbor bonds only, 7878 further TRS states have them, among them the (π,0,0)(\pi,0,0) state U0111-2. The chiral state ℬ\mathcal{B}:SU000-000, which is not counted among them, is another example. At Point A, no state outside the ζ=−\zeta=- PSGs keeps a flat band at the Fermi level.

Spin structure factors of all states, computed from the mean-field two-spinon bubble with the actual site positions, are given in Sec. SIV of the SM, with representative examples in Fig. S1. Apart from the flat-band states, whose structure factor takes amplitude-independent values in the grand-canonical T→0+T\to 0^{+} mean-field ensemble, in which the zero modes are half filled (a state at fixed particle number or a projected state need not share these values), they show broad maxima of similar height, 0.150.15 to 0.190.19, for all spectral types, so that the static structure factor alone does not distinguish them.

VIII Spin–Orbit Coupling

Spin–orbit coupling allows spin-dependent spinon hopping and pairing, the triplet links of Eq. (7). Their allowed directions on each bond are fixed by the PSG through Eq. (9). This section states two symmetry results for the mean-field spinon Hamiltonian and the topological spinon bands they allow, and Sec. VIII.3 discusses what happens beyond mean-field theory. Symmetry classes are given in Appendix D, and the full survey and further examples in Sec. SV of the SM.

VIII.1 Projective Moriya Rule

Moriya’s rules [77] determine the allowed directions of a Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya (DM) vector from the symmetries that leave a bond invariant, using the spin rotations RgR_{g} of Appendix A.2. For spinon links, each of these symmetries also carries a PSG sign. To see its effect, regard the singlet link qi​j0=−i​ui​j(0)q^{0}_{ij}=-\mathrm{i}u^{(0)}_{ij} and the triplet links qi​ja=ui​j(a)q^{a}_{ij}=u^{(a)}_{ij} as real quaternions, and form the vector vi​ja=⟨qi​j0,qi​ja⟩v^{a}_{ij}=\langle q^{0}_{ij},q^{a}_{ij}\rangle. The PSG sign multiplies both links, so it cancels in vi​jav^{a}_{ij}. This vector therefore transforms exactly like a DM vector and obeys Moriya’s rules on every bond, in every PSG.

Apparent violations can occur only on bonds where the PSG forbids the singlet hopping, so that vi​jav^{a}_{ij} vanishes. There the triplet links can point in directions that Moriya’s rules would not allow. In the class U0001-0, for example, the bonds JdJ_{d}, Jb​sJ_{bs}, J×J_{\times}, and J+J_{+} carry no singlet hopping and an out-of-plane DM-like vector, where Moriya’s rule requires an in-plane one (Appendix D). This concerns the spinon ansatz only, since the DM vectors of the physical spin Hamiltonian always obey Moriya’s rules.

VIII.2 Spinon Quantum Spin Hall States

With spin–orbit coupling, a gapped spinon band structure can be a quantum spin Hall insulator, with a nontrivial ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} invariant (ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}-odd) and helical edge modes. Among the U⁡(1)U(1) and S​U​(2)SU(2) PSGs, this is possible only in the 3232 U⁡(1)U(1) PSGs with wΘ=1w_{\Theta}=1. These conserve spinon number and have Θ2=−1\Theta^{2}=-1 on the spinons, which places them in symmetry class AII [3, 99] (Appendix D.2). The ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} PSGs with spin–orbit coupling belong to class DIII and are not studied here.

Two rules restrict where such states can occur.

  • •

    Charge conjugation. If spin–orbit coupling conserves SzS^{z}, the spin Chern number C↑C_{\uparrow} vanishes whenever a symmetry exchanges spinon particles and holes (wTw_{T}, wC4w_{C_{4}}, or wσw_{\sigma} equal to 11). Such a symmetry maps the occupied bands of one spin species onto the empty bands of a spin species, which reverses the Chern number twice, through the exchange of occupied and empty bands and through complex conjugation. A translation or C4C_{4}, which keeps SzS^{z}, maps spin up onto spin down and gives C↓=C↑C_{\downarrow}=C_{\uparrow}, which together with C↓=−C↑C_{\downarrow}=-C_{\uparrow} from time reversal forces C↑=0C_{\uparrow}=0. The mirror σ\sigma, whose spin rotation reverses SzS^{z}, maps spin up onto itself and reverses the orientation of the lattice, which gives C↑=−C↑C_{\uparrow}=-C_{\uparrow} directly. With conserved SzS^{z}, spinon quantum spin Hall states are therefore possible only in the four classes U0001-nn.

  • •

    Forced zero modes. Some states cannot be gapped at all: the flat-band PSGs, whose zero modes (Sec. IV.3) survive any allowed spin–orbit coupling, and nine further U⁡(1)U(1) classes in which every ansatz has exact zero modes at a time-reversal-invariant momentum (Appendix D.2).

Gapped ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}-odd states do occur (Fig. 5). State Q1 belongs to the class U0001-2. Its singlet parent, uniform hopping on J1J_{1} and J23J_{23}, is the flux state (0,0,0)(0,0,0) of Table 5. With the multipliers fixed by ⟨ni⟩=1\langle n_{i}\rangle=1, its highest occupied band lies at the Fermi level along the lines k1=0k_{1}=0 and k2=0k_{2}=0, and the lowest empty band touches it quadratically at Γ\Gamma, where the lines cross. An out-of-plane DM term on the square edges gaps both, linear in its strength, and gives one helical pair per edge [Fig. 5(a), (b)]. State Q2, in the class U0001-0, is gapped in the same way by a DM term on the bow-tie edges. Its bands satisfy E⁡(𝒌)=E⁡(𝒌+(π,π))E(\bm{k})=E(\bm{k}+(\pi,\pi)) [Fig. 5(c)], a direct signature of its projective PSG (Appendix D.2).

With generic spin–orbit coupling, ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}-odd states also occur in the staggered gauge sectors (wT=1w_{T}=1). There the translations exchange spinon particles and holes, and a translation combined with time reversal acts as a chiral symmetry that pins the Fermi level at E=0E=0. State S1, in U1101-3, has a spectrum that is symmetric under E→−EE\to-E and twofold degenerate at every momentum [Fig. 5(d)]. On a ribbon, one Kramers pair per edge crosses E=0E=0 [Fig. 5(e)].

A survey of all 3232 AII classes (Sec. SV of the SM) confirms these rules. With conserved SzS^{z}, ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}-odd states occur only in U0001-0 and U0001-2. With generic spin–orbit coupling, they also occur in the staggered gauge sectors and, rarely, in U0111-2.

VIII.3 Beyond Mean-Field Theory

These spinon insulators are not stable spin liquids. With conserved SzS^{z}, time reversal forbids a Chern–Simons term for the emergent gauge field, but the monopoles of the gauge field carry spin Sz=C↑S^{z}=C_{\uparrow}, as charge is carried by skyrmions in quantum spin Hall insulators [32, 88]. If no other gapless matter is present, the monopoles therefore cannot enter the action, the gauge field becomes the Goldstone mode of broken spin rotation about 𝒛^\hat{\bm{z}}, and the physical state orders. Its order parameter carries Sz=C↑S^{z}=C_{\uparrow}: an in-plane magnetic moment for |C↑|=1|C_{\uparrow}|=1, a spin-nematic for |C↑|=2|C_{\uparrow}|=2, and (S+)3(S^{+})^{3} for |C↑|=3|C_{\uparrow}|=3. Its spatial pattern depends on the lattice quantum numbers of the monopoles, which we have not determined.

With generic spin–orbit coupling the monopoles are allowed, and the U⁡(1)U(1) gauge field confines [84]. A stable state then requires spinon pairing, which reduces the gauge group to ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} and leads to class DIII [51], and we do not study these states here. Even then, the protected spinon edges need not survive, because pairing can gap a helical spinon edge. If the state confines instead, the constraint of Sec. X, which we expect but do not prove for time reversal alone, would forbid a featureless symmetric paramagnet, so that the confined state breaks a symmetry or is gapless.

IX Noncoplanar Orders and Chiral Spin Liquids

We now return to the question: which chiral liquids can the noncoplanar orders of the cross-octagon model [26] produce, and does the energetics favor one? We first find the classical phases (Sec. IX.1) and the chiral class that each order would pass on to a liquid (Secs. IX.2 and IX.3). We then compare candidate states in self-consistent mean-field theory (Sec. IX.4) and with projected wave functions (Sec. IX.5).

IX.1 Classical Phases of the Cross-Octagon Model

We study the Heisenberg model with equal nearest-neighbor couplings J1=J2=J3=±1J_{1}=J_{2}=J_{3}=\pm 1 and couplings J+J_{+} and J×J_{\times} across the octagons [26]. To find exact classical ground states, we use the Luttinger–Tisza (LT) method [64, 65, 49] with one Lagrange multiplier per site orbit. It gives a lower bound on the energy, and a spin state that reaches the bound is a ground state.

For antiferromagnetic nearest neighbors, the bound is reached by the order cuboc1 for J+,J×≥0J_{+},J_{\times}\geq 0, and by a degenerate family of 2​π/32\pi/3 states, with 120∘120^{\circ} between the three spins of every triangle, for J+,J×≤0J_{+},J_{\times}\leq 0 [Fig. 6(a), with the energies in Eq. (32)]. For ferromagnetic nearest neighbors, the bound is reached everywhere, by ferromagnetic, octagonal, and conical orders, with the phase boundaries (J×−1)​(J+−1)=1/2(J_{\times}-1)(J_{+}-1)=1/2 and (J×+1/2)​(J++1/2)=1(J_{\times}+1/\sqrt{2})(J_{+}+1/\sqrt{2})=1 [Fig. 6(d)]. These results agree with the closed forms of Ref. [26].

In the two quadrants with J+​J×<0J_{+}J_{\times}<0 the bound is not reached. There, simulated annealing on large and twisted cells finds incommensurate noncoplanar states [Fig. 6(b)]. They are the lowest states we found, but without a reached bound they carry no certificate of global optimality. This refines Ref. [26] in two ways. First, the regular orders of its phases II and VII, which we call cuboc-d and 2​π/32\pi/3-d, are ground states only on the line J×=0J_{\times}=0. Away from it, long-wavelength modulations of them have lower energy [Fig. 6(c)], with periods that grow as 1/|J×|1/|J_{\times}| and are too long to fit on the finite clusters of Ref. [26]. Second, the spiral states of its phases III, IV, V, VIII, IX, and X are not the lowest states: incommensurate states lie slightly lower. Details are given in Sec. SVII of the SM.

Phase II has two degenerate regular orders, built from the irreducible blocks B2+M5B_{2}+M_{5} (88 spin directions) and M4+M5M_{4}+M_{5} (1212 directions). We call them cuboc-d and cuboc-d′. Figure 7 shows the commensurate orders.

IX.2 Regular Orders and Chiral Classes

In a regular order, every lattice symmetry gg can be undone by a global spin rotation Rg∈O⁡(3)R_{g}\in O(3) [72]. If detRg=−1\det R_{g}=-1, this rotation includes a spin inversion, so in a liquid that keeps the symmetry of the order, gg appears only together with time reversal. The order thus passes on the chiral class

ϵ⁡(g)=detRg\epsilon(g)=\det R_{g} (24)

of Sec. III.4. This assumes that the liquid keeps the magnetic symmetry of its parent order, a mean-field heuristic rather than a theorem. A liquid that breaks further symmetries is not constrained by Eq. (24).

Table 8 gives the result for the orders of the cross-octagon model. None of them falls into class ℬ\mathcal{B}, so none allows a Chern number. Their scalar chirality alternates in space, under a translation or under the fourfold rotation, and their net chirality is zero. cuboc1 and its partner cuboc3 also break the fourfold rotation and the diagonal mirrors. Their magnetic group is the nematic group p​2​m​mp2mm, in which T1T_{1} is combined with time reversal [Fig. 7(j)].22 2 Reference [26] remarks that its noncoplanar orders are not regular. This holds for cuboc1 and the spirals, while the cuboc-d and conical orders are regular under the full group p​4​m​mp4mm. We state the result as a selection rule: a phase that keeps the magnetic group of a noncoplanar parent order has C=0C=0 and κx​y=0\kappa_{xy}=0 whenever that group contains an element gg with ϵ⁡(g)​det(g)=−1\epsilon(g)\det(g)=-1, such as a translation or rotation combined with time reversal. It follows from Sec. VI.2 and needs only the magnetic group. Its one assumption is that the liquid inherits this group. It does not constrain a liquid that spontaneously breaks the Hall-reversing element, as a uniformly chiral liquid would.

Uniformly chiral orders of class ℬ\mathcal{B} do exist. With magnetic cells of up to 2×22\times 2 unit cells there are 3434 families of noncoplanar regular orders, and 1717 of them have exact parent Hamiltonians with couplings up to J+J_{+} (Appendix E). Three of these are in class ℬ\mathcal{B}: A1+M5A_{1}+M_{5}, M1+X4M_{1}+X_{4}, and M4+X1M_{4}+X_{1}. They have a uniform chirality on the nearest-neighbor triangles, but their parent Hamiltonians need ferromagnetic bow-tie couplings and sizable further-neighbor couplings, far from the antiferromagnetic regime considered here. We have not studied their quantum melting, nor searched for uniformly chiral orders that are not regular, such as incommensurate ones, so the need for ferromagnetic bow-tie couplings is established only for the regular orders.

For each order of Table 8 we also identified the PSGs that reproduce its chirality pattern. For cuboc-d these are class-𝒟\mathcal{D} PSGs such as 𝒟\mathcal{D}:SU011-001. For the conical order, the natural candidate 𝒟′\mathcal{D}^{\prime}:U100-0 is gapped with C=0C=0, as it must be.

IX.3 Nematic PSGs of the Cuboc1 Class

A liquid that keeps the symmetry of cuboc1 is invariant under T2T_{2}, the two axial mirrors σx\sigma_{x} and σy\sigma_{y}, and T1​ΘT_{1}\Theta, and breaks the fourfold rotation. Since T1T_{1} and T2T_{2} are treated differently, this is not one of the chiral classes of p​4​m​mp4mm. We therefore classified the PSGs of the smaller group p​2​m​mp2mm (Sec. SX of the SM). It gives 100100 ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}, 4848 discrete U⁡(1)U(1) and one flux family, and 44 S​U​(2)SU(2) PSGs.

To reproduce the chirality pattern of cuboc1, which sits on the half-square triangles, a state needs the square diagonals JdJ_{d} in addition to the nearest-neighbor bonds. This is possible in 5858 ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} and 77 U⁡(1)U(1) PSGs, and in no S​U​(2)SU(2) PSG. A natural candidate is N:U1000-0, which reproduces the chirality of cuboc1 on all loops up to J+J_{+}. With nearest-neighbor and JdJ_{d} amplitudes it is gapped, with Δ=0.156\Delta=0.156, and has C=0C=0, as T1​ΘT_{1}\Theta requires. These fermionic states complement the nematic spin liquid found in Schwinger-boson theory of a related model [63].

IX.4 Self-Consistent Mean-Field States

To see which state a Heisenberg model selects at mean-field level, we solved the self-consistency equations of the model of Ref. [26] with J1=J2=J3=1J_{1}=J_{2}=J_{3}=1 at eight points: the nearest-neighbor point A0, four points C1a–C1d in the cuboc1 phase, and three points CDa–CDc in phase II (Table 9 and Fig. 8). The on-site constraints are imposed by site-dependent multipliers.

Unprojected mean-field theory has a known bias. Each bond contributes ⟨𝑺i⋅𝑺j⟩=−38​(|χi​j|2+|pi​j|2)\langle\bm{S}_{i}\cdot\bm{S}_{j}\rangle=-\frac{3}{8}(|\chi_{ij}|^{2}+|p_{ij}|^{2}), with χi​j\chi_{ij} and pi​jp_{ij} the hopping and pairing expectation values, and the lowest possible energy, −3/16-3/16 per site at all eight points, is reached by isolated dimers and four-site clusters. These break the lattice symmetries and say nothing about the classical phases. We therefore compare only symmetric states whose bonds connect the whole lattice, each solved within its PSG. This comparison diagnoses the PSG manifolds, whereas the physical ranking requires projection (Sec. IX.5). At C1a–C1d we solved all S​U​(2)SU(2) and U⁡(1)U(1) PSGs and a sample of ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} PSGs in each class, and at the other points fewer candidates. All solved manifolds and their energies are in the SM.

The self-consistent solutions do not inherit the class of the melted cuboc1 order. Among the connected symmetric states, the lowest at A0 and C1a–C1d is the class-ℬ\mathcal{B} state ℬ\mathcal{B}:SU011-001 of Sec. VI.3, with its flux pattern, S​U​(2)SU(2) gauge group, and Chern number unchanged. It is also the lowest of the fewer candidates at CDa–CDc. The self-consistency map flows to it from many starting points, but it is a saddle point: one soft distortion, which breaks the fourfold rotation, lowers the energy towards a dimer covering. The closest connected competitor is a gapless class-ℬ′\mathcal{B}^{\prime} state, lying higher in energy by 0.0040.004–0.0100.010. The best TRS states are higher by 0.0060.006–0.0130.013, and the states of the nematic class and of classes 𝒟\mathcal{D} and 𝒟′\mathcal{D}^{\prime} lie higher still (Sec. SVIII of the SM). At the nearest-neighbor point, this ranking agrees with Ref. [4].

At four of the eight points, a state that is not two-dimensional lies lower: π\pi-flux squares and decoupled chains of bow-tie sites along the J+J_{+} bonds, with energy E/N=−1/8−J+/(2π2)E/N=-1/8-J_{+}/(2\pi^{2}) (Table 9). We list it separately. The mean-field structure factor of the class-ℬ\mathcal{B} state at C1b (Fig. S2 of the SM) has its maxima close to the Bragg peaks of cuboc1, so the static structure factor alone cannot distinguish the chiral liquid from short-range cuboc1 correlations.

These are unprojected results. Already at the nearest-neighbor point, projection places three nonchiral flux states and two valence-bond crystals below the class-ℬ\mathcal{B} state [4]. For the ferromagnetic regimes of cuboc3 and the conical order, singlet mean-field theory is not meaningful.

IX.5 Projected Wave Functions

Method. To rank the physical spin-1/21/2 states, we compared Gutzwiller-projected wave functions [33, 31] along the cuboc1 line J+=J×=λJ_{+}=J_{\times}=\lambda, which passes through C1a (λ=0.5\lambda=0.5) and C1b (λ=1\lambda=1). The wave functions are projected Slater determinants, optimized by stochastic reconfiguration [106, 107, 7]. We compare:

  • •

    the PSG spin liquids of Sec. IX.4: the class-ℬ\mathcal{B} S​U​(2)SU(2) and ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} states, the TRS state Z000-011-100(1), and two states of the nematic group, N:Z00000-101 (TRS) and N:Z00000-110 (the nematic chiral state),

  • •

    a cuboc1-ordered state, obtained by adding a field −h𝒏i⋅𝝈-h\,\bm{n}_{i}\cdot\bm{\sigma} along the classical cuboc1 directions 𝒏i\bm{n}_{i},

  • •

    a valence-bond crystal with free hopping on all bonds of the 2×22\times 2 magnetic cell, and

  • •

    a combination of the crystal and the cuboc1 field.

Energies are averaged over boundary twists [55], computed on clusters of 9696 to 600600 sites, and extrapolated in 1/N1/N. For the crystal and the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} states these fits have large χ2\chi^{2} per degree of freedom, because their energies scatter between clusters beyond the statistical errors. We therefore base the ranking primarily on the differences on the largest common cluster (Table S7 of the SM) and treat the extrapolated values of Table 10 as secondary, and both give the same ranking. The quoted errors are statistical. The scatter between local optima of the optimization, which is one-sided because the lowest optimum is kept, and the spread over fit forms are discussed in Sec. SIX of the SM. The variational families also differ in flexibility: the crystal has 6363 free parameters, the PSG states 33 to 1111, the nematic states 1818 and 2626, and the ordered state 44, and only the ordered state receives a Jastrow factor (Table S6 of the SM). The comparison ranks these families and does not determine the exact phase diagram. Two independent codes agree, and the projected energies of Ref. [4] at the nearest-neighbor point are reproduced. Details are given in Sec. SIX of the SM.

Along the cuboc1 line (Table 10, Fig. 9). For λ≥0.4\lambda\geq 0.4 the cuboc1-ordered state lies below every spin liquid, and its order survives in the thermodynamic limit, with m2=0.07m^{2}=0.07 to 0.130.13 (the classical value is 1/41/4). For λ≤0.3\lambda\leq 0.3 the order melts during optimization. At weaker couplings a valence-bond crystal is lowest. It has a pinwheel pattern, with strong dimers around half of the squares and resonating squares on the other half (Fig. S3 of the SM). Within these variational spaces, the crystal and the ordered state cross near λc≈0.5\lambda_{c}\approx 0.5, between 0.50.5 and 0.550.55. Near the crossing, independent starts of the crystal optimization agree within 1.5×10−41.5\times 10^{-4} on 216216 sites, but the location of the crossing depends on further optimization and on correlation factors. A Jastrow factor for the ordered state lowers its energy by up to 2×10−32\times 10^{-3} per site and makes the two energies equal at C1a. Since both energies are variational upper bounds, λc\lambda_{c} can move either way: a better crystal would move it up, and an S​U​(2)SU(2)-invariant Jastrow factor, which usually favors order, would move it down.

No chiral state is lowest at any λ\lambda. The class-ℬ\mathcal{B} states lie above the ordered state at every λ\lambda computed. The ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} state of class ℬ\mathcal{B} comes within 0.0030.003 of the best spin liquid for 0.4≤λ≤0.50.4\leq\lambda\leq 0.5, but only by giving up its chirality. Its optimized amplitudes carry a weak time-reversal-odd flux, |sin⁡Φ△|≤0.1|\sin\Phi_{\triangle}|\leq 0.1 on the triangles, compared with 11 in the S​U​(2)SU(2) state, and its projected scalar chirality falls with the cluster size, at λ=0.5\lambda=0.5 from 0.0530.053 on 9696 sites to 0.0110.011 on 384384 sites (Table S8 of the SM). Its energy is therefore no evidence for a nearby chiral phase. The S​U​(2)SU(2) state keeps its chirality but lies 0.030.03 to 0.060.06 above the ordered state. The nematic chiral state N:Z00000-110, the liquid that would inherit the symmetry of cuboc1, lies 0.0250.025 to 0.050.05 above the best spin liquid. This differs from the kagome lattice, where variational and density-matrix renormalization group studies find uniformly chiral liquids near the cuboc orders [9, 8, 39, 27, 118]. At C1b the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} energies depend strongly on the boundary twist, and the ranking of the spin liquids there is not settled.

Across the phase boundary. On the kagome lattice, chiral liquids appear where classical phases meet [118]. We therefore also followed a cut at J+=1J_{+}=1 from J×=0.5J_{\times}=0.5 to −0.1-0.1, into phase II, on clusters of up to 384384 sites. The cuboc1 order does not melt along this cut, but it is overtaken by nonchiral states. On 384384 sites a valence-bond crystal is lowest at J×=0.5J_{\times}=0.5, 0.0060.006 below the ordered state, and for J×≤0.25J_{\times}\leq 0.25 the TRS state Z000-011-100(1), 0.00130.0013 to 0.00190.0019 below the crystal, a margin too small to establish a spin-liquid phase there. Both are close to a product of singlet squares and Heisenberg chains along J+J_{+}, with ⟨𝑺i⋅𝑺j⟩≈−0.47\langle\bm{S}_{i}\cdot\bm{S}_{j}\rangle\approx-0.47 on the square edges, −0.39-0.39 to −0.41-0.41 on the J+J_{+} bonds, and −0.04-0.04 to −0.05-0.05 on the bow-tie edges. In that product state the bonds between squares and chains and the J×J_{\times} bonds carry no energy, so it has the energy

Eprod/N=−[2+2J+(ln2−14)]/6E_{\rm prod}/N=-\big[2+2J_{+}(\ln 2-\tfrac{1}{4})\big]/6 (25)

for any J×J_{\times}, −0.4810-0.4810 at J+=1J_{+}=1, an upper bound on the ground-state energy that does not depend on our wave functions. The lowest projected states lie below it, at E/N=−0.506E/N=-0.506 to −0.508-0.508 on 384384 sites, 0.0250.025 to 0.0270.027 lower, whereas the ordered state lies above it for J×≤0.25J_{\times}\leq 0.25. Along the line J+=J×J_{+}=J_{\times} the lowest states lie 0.050.05 to 0.090.09 below EprodE_{\rm prod} (Table S7 of the SM). The class-ℬ\mathcal{B} S​U​(2)SU(2) state falls below the ordered state for J×≤0.25J_{\times}\leq 0.25 but stays 0.0150.015 to 0.0170.017 above the lowest state, and the nematic and class-𝒟\mathcal{D} chiral states lose their chirality during optimization.

Through the nearest-neighbor point. Continued to λ=0.2\lambda=0.2, 0.10.1, −0.1-0.1, −0.2-0.2, and −0.3-0.3, into the quadrant of the 2​π/32\pi/3 manifold, the line J+=J×=λJ_{+}=J_{\times}=\lambda has the crystal lowest at every point on clusters of up to 384384 sites, with the TRS state Z000-011-100(1) 0.0010.001 to 0.0040.004 and the best chiral state, the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} state of class ℬ\mathcal{B}, 0.0140.014 to 0.0180.018 above it. The cuboc1 and coplanar 2​π/32\pi/3 orders melt near λ=0\lambda=0, and the 2​π/32\pi/3 order that survives at λ=−0.3\lambda=-0.3 lies 0.0090.009 above the crystal.

Limitations. These comparisons are variational and limited to the states considered. Unbiased methods are not available here: the smallest cluster that fits the 2×22\times 2 cells has 2424 sites and maps the J+J_{+} bonds onto each other. Crystals on larger cells, other starting patterns, S​U​(2)SU(2)-invariant Jastrow factors, and coexistence of dimerization and order could shift the boundaries.

X Stability and the Lieb–Schultz–Mattis-Type Constraint

We end with what symmetry says about the physical state. With six spins per unit cell, the Lieb–Schultz–Mattis theorem [54, 81, 35] gives no constraint on the square-kagome lattice, but lattice homotopy [82] does. Assume spin-rotation symmetry, or just its π\pi rotations. Each bow-tie site is a twofold rotation center carrying a spin 1/21/2, and this spin cannot be moved away without breaking a symmetry. The four square sites of a cell, by contrast, can be moved along their mirror lines to the square center, where together they carry integer spin. The lattice is therefore equivalent to the checkerboard lattice, and it has no symmetric, gapped ground state without topological order. This agrees with the valence-bond crystals found numerically, which break lattice symmetries [94, 97, 44]. With time reversal alone, as for generic spin–orbit coupling, each bow-tie spin is a Kramers doublet, and similar constraints are expected [114, 82], although we do not prove them here.

This constraint acts on the projected state. It combines with the stability of the mean-field states as follows. Gapped U⁡(1)U(1) and S​U​(2)SU(2) states without a Chern–Simons term confine in two dimensions [84]. Stable spin liquids among our states are therefore (i) the gapped ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} states, (ii) the chiral states with C≠0C\neq 0, such as the class-ℬ\mathcal{B} state, whose Chern–Simons term gaps the gauge field, and (iii) the Dirac spin liquids, if their fermion bilinears and monopoles are harmless, which we do not check [37, 103, 102]. Only (i) and (ii) are gapped, symmetric, and compatible with the constraint. A gapped U⁡(1)U(1) state with C=0C=0 must, when it confines, either break a lattice symmetry or close its gap. This holds for the gapped TRS U⁡(1)U(1) states of Sec. VII.3, the gapped C=0C=0 states of Sec. IX.4 outside the primed classes, and the nematic candidate N:U1000-0 of Sec. IX.3.

The argument relies only on the unitarity of the twofold rotations about the bow-tie sites. The rotation C42C_{4}^{2} about the square center is unitary in every class (Sec. VI.2), but the bow-tie rotations T1​C42T_{1}C_{4}^{2} and T2​C42T_{2}C_{4}^{2} carry the character ϵT\epsilon_{T}. In the nematic class of cuboc1, ϵ⁡(T1)=−1\epsilon(T_{1})=-1, so the rotation about the sites μ=5\mu=5 is combined with time reversal. The sites μ=6\mu=6 still suffice: they are centers of the unitary rotation T2​C42T_{2}C_{4}^{2} of the subgroup {T12,T2,σx,σy}\{T_{1}^{2},T_{2},\sigma_{x},\sigma_{y}\}, whose unit cell is doubled, and each carries a spin 1/21/2. In the other nematic domain the sites 55 and 66 swap roles. In the staggered classes 𝒜′\mathcal{A}^{\prime}–𝒟′\mathcal{D}^{\prime} both bow-tie rotations are combined with time reversal, and the argument does not apply in this form.

XI Conclusions and Outlook

Both site orbits of the square-kagome lattice have nontrivial site symmetry, and this shapes its fermionic spin liquids. The site symmetries reduce the cohomology classes to the algebraic PSGs of Sec. IV. The relative sign ζ\zeta of time reversal on the two orbits decides which PSGs are realizable. For ζ=+\zeta=+ no amplitude survives. For ζ=−\zeta=- only square–bow-tie bonds survive, and the spinon bands are exactly flat at the Fermi level (Sec. IV.3). These flat bands are the zero modes of the bipartite square–bow-tie graph, which has twice as many square sites as bow-tie sites [109, 53]. Two further features make the chiral states richer than on the kagome lattice. The lattice contains triangles, so chiral states appear already with nearest-neighbor bonds. Its translations can be combined with time reversal, which gives staggered chiral classes that do not exist with sixfold symmetry [74].

Only class ℬ\mathcal{B} allows a Chern number. Its nearest-neighbor S​U​(2)SU(2) state is gapped with C=±1C=\pm 1, a mean-field Kalmeyer–Laughlin state (Sec. VI.3). The cuboc and conical orders of the cross-octagon model fall into other classes. A liquid that keeps the magnetic symmetry of such an order therefore has a chirality that alternates in space, and C=0C=0. This rule does not forbid chiral liquids; it forbids only a spontaneous thermal Hall response in a liquid inherited from these orders. The energetics also does not favor a chiral liquid. Unprojected mean-field theory ranks the class-ℬ\mathcal{B} state lowest among the symmetric two-dimensional states we solved, but projection reverses this. Among the projected states we compared, the cuboc1 order is lowest for strong cross-octagon couplings and a pinwheel valence-bond crystal for weaker ones along J+=J×J_{+}=J_{\times}. Across the cuboc1 phase boundary a TRS ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} state and the crystal, both close to decoupled squares and chains and 0.0250.025 below the energy of that product state, are lowest within 0.0020.002 of each other. The class-ℬ\mathcal{B} states and the nematic chiral state lie higher at every coupling we computed, including a cut across the cuboc1 phase boundary and the continuation of the line J+=J×J_{+}=J_{\times} through the nearest-neighbor point (Sec. IX.5). This differs from the kagome lattice, where uniformly chiral liquids are found near the cuboc orders [9, 8, 39, 27, 118].

Uniformly chiral class-ℬ\mathcal{B} regular orders do exist on the square-kagome lattice, but those we found need ferromagnetic bow-tie couplings and further-neighbor couplings beyond those of Ref. [26], and nonregular ones remain to be explored. A spontaneous zero-field thermal Hall signal from spinons would therefore point to a uniformly chiral liquid, not to a melted cuboc or conical order. In experiments, such a signal must be separated from field-induced magnon and phonon contributions [113, 18, 30] and from averaging over chiral domains.

The flat bands of the ζ=−\zeta=- states and the symmetry selection rules hold for all amplitudes. Spectral types, Dirac cone numbers, and Chern numbers were determined at chosen amplitudes, and mapping them across the amplitude space is a natural next step. The self-consistent treatment can be extended to all ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} PSGs, to magnetic cells larger than 2×22\times 2, and to magnetically ordered mean-field states, and the projected comparison to Jastrow factors for the spin liquids as well as for the ordered state. Structure factors, edge states, and thermal Hall responses were computed for mean-field spinons, and evaluating them in the projected states will include the effect of gauge fluctuations. Finally, real materials have lower symmetry than p​4​m​mp4mm, through inequivalent bow-tie edges, buckling, or decorating sites, and the same classification scheme applies to these subgroups.

These results point to several directions. Interactions and gauge fluctuations will lift the large degeneracy of the flat bands, and it will be interesting to see whether the resulting states connect to the valence-bond crystals found numerically [94, 4, 97, 44], for instance through the fermion bilinears and monopoles of the Dirac states [37, 103, 102]. Two refinements will pin down the crystal–cuboc1 boundary at λc≈0.5\lambda_{c}\approx 0.5–0.550.55: larger crystal cells and the loop-six and crossed-dimer patterns of Refs. [4, 97], which would move it up, and S​U​(2)SU(2)-invariant Jastrow factors [7, 42], which usually favor order and would move it down. By the constraint of Sec. X, any gapped symmetric state found there must be topologically ordered. Finally, a Schwinger-boson classification, building on Ref. [63], would cover spin liquids next to the noncoplanar orders, and the nematic and staggered classes found here provide its symmetry framework.

The data that support the findings of this article, including the canonical forms of all projective symmetry groups, the amplitudes, spectra, and structure factors of all realized spin liquids, and the data of the noncoplanar orders and variational calculations, are openly available on Zenodo as part of the SM [86].

Appendix A Conventions and Fermion Bilinears

A.1 Conventions

A site is labeled i=(x,y,μ)i=(x,y,\mu) (Sec. II), and the generators act on the labels by Eq. (3), while time reversal Θ\Theta fixes every site. Words in the generators are read from right to left. By Eq. (11) a word O1O2⋯OnO_{1}O_{2}\cdots O_{n} is represented by

where a letter Ok=O−1O_{k}=O^{-1} contributes GO−1​(ik−1)=[GO​(O⁡(ik−1))]−1G_{O^{-1}}(i_{k-1})=[G_{O}(O(i_{k-1}))]^{-1}. If a word equals the identity of the symmetry group, GO1⋯On(i)G_{O_{1}\cdots O_{n}}(i) lies in the IGG and, in the canonical gauge, in which the IGG consists of site-independent matrices, does not depend on ii. We call it the value of the relation. For IGG ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} the values of the relations (4) are the signs η\eta of Eq. (16), each equal to ±τ0\pm\tau^{0} and identified with ±1\pm 1. Two sets {GO}\{G_{O}\} describe the same PSG if they are related by a gauge transformation

Under Eq. (27) the inner factors of Eq. (26) cancel pairwise, and since a relation returns to its starting site its value η\eta becomes Wi​η​Wi†=ηW_{i}\eta W_{i}^{\dagger}=\eta, so relation values are gauge invariant. A re-lifting GO→−GOG_{O}\to-G_{O} multiplies the value of a relation by (−1)NO(-1)^{N_{O}}, where NON_{O} is the number of letters OO or O−1O^{-1} in the word. Fluxes are oriented counterclockwise, the hopping ti​jt_{ij} is the coefficient of fi​σ†​fj​σf^{\dagger}_{i\sigma}f_{j\sigma}, and the Berry connection is 𝓐=i​∑n⟨un|∇𝒌un⟩\bm{\mathcal{A}}=\mathrm{i}\sum_{n}\langle u_{n}|\nabla_{\bm{k}}u_{n}\rangle over the occupied bands (Sec. VI.2). The hopping flux of a triangle, Φ=arg⁡(t12​t23​t31)\Phi=\arg(t_{12}t_{23}t_{31}) for 1→2→31\to 2\to 3 counterclockwise, is minus the Aharonov–Bohm phase of a spinon encircling the triangle counterclockwise. A.2 Spin Rotations

With spin–orbit coupling a lattice operation rotates the spin by the rotation part of the operation acting on an axial vector, in which a mirror acts as the twofold rotation about its normal. In the frame (𝒙^,𝒚^,𝒛^)(\hat{\bm{x}},\hat{\bm{y}},\hat{\bm{z}}) of Eq. (1), with 𝒛^\hat{\bm{z}} normal to the layer, the matrices ROR_{O} of Eq. (9) are

Rσ\displaystyle R_{\sigma} =(0−10−10000−1),\displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1&0\\ -1&0&0\\ 0&0&-1\end{pmatrix}, (28)

where RC4R_{C_{4}} is the rotation by π/2\pi/2 about 𝒛^\hat{\bm{z}} and RσR_{\sigma} the twofold rotation about the normal (1,−1,0)/2(1,-1,0)/\sqrt{2} of the mirror line X=YX=Y.
