Appendix B Derivation of the Projective Symmetry Groups

B.1 Canonical Gauge

We fix the gauge in three steps. A gauge transformation sets GT1=τ0G_{T_{1}}=\tau^{0} on all sites and GT2=τ0G_{T_{2}}=\tau^{0} on the line x=0x=0, and the relation T2​T1​T2−1​T1−1=η12T_{2}T_{1}T_{2}^{-1}T_{1}^{-1}=\eta_{12} then gives GT2​(x,y,μ)=η12x​τ0G_{T_{2}}(x,y,\mu)=\eta_{12}^{x}\tau^{0}. The relations that fix the action of the point group on the translations, C4​T1​C4−1​T2−1C_{4}T_{1}C_{4}^{-1}T_{2}^{-1}, C4​T2​C4−1​T1C_{4}T_{2}C_{4}^{-1}T_{1}, σ​T1​σ−1​T2−1\sigma T_{1}\sigma^{-1}T_{2}^{-1}, and σ​T2​σ−1​T1−1\sigma T_{2}\sigma^{-1}T_{1}^{-1}, and the commutators of the translations with Θ\Theta then determine the dependence of GC4G_{C_{4}}, GσG_{\sigma}, and GΘG_{\Theta} on (x,y)(x,y) up to the signs of Eq. (15), which are relation values. The relation C4​T1​C4−1​T2−1C_{4}T_{1}C_{4}^{-1}T_{2}^{-1} is set to +1+1 by re-lifting T1T_{1}. Since C4−1C_{4}^{-1} maps the cell (x,y)(x,y) to (y,−x)(y,-x) up to a shift for the bow-tie sites, which does not change the sign of GT2G_{T_{2}}, the forms hold for all six sublattices. A remaining gauge freedom on the sublattices sets gC4​(μ)g_{C_{4}}(\mu) to a fixed value along a spanning tree of the C4C_{4} action on the sublattices, μ=2,3,4\mu=2,3,4 and 66, so that gC4​(1)g_{C_{4}}(1) and gC4​(5)g_{C_{4}}(5) carry the relation C44C_{4}^{4} on the two orbits: gC4​(μ)=τ0g_{C_{4}}(\mu)=\tau^{0} for the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} and S​U​(2)SU(2) PSGs and for the U⁡(1)U(1) PSGs with wC4=0w_{C_{4}}=0, and gC4​(μ)=i​τ1g_{C_{4}}(\mu)=\mathrm{i}\tau^{1} for the U⁡(1)U(1) PSGs with wC4=1w_{C_{4}}=1, in which every GC4​(i)G_{C_{4}}(i) reverses the U⁡(1)U(1) rotation.

Every site stabilizer of p​4​m​m×ℤ2Θp4mm\times\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{\Theta} is an elementary abelian 22-group: ⟨T1​C42,σ​C4,Θ⟩≅ℤ23\langle T_{1}C_{4}^{2},\sigma C_{4},\Theta\rangle\cong\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{3} for the bow-tie site (0,0,5)(0,0,5) and ⟨σ,Θ⟩≅ℤ22\langle\sigma,\Theta\rangle\cong\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{2} for the square site (0,0,1)(0,0,1). The images of their projective S​U​(2)SU(2) representations lie, after a global rotation on each orbit, in the quaternion group {±τ0,±i​τ1,±i​τ2,±i​τ3}\{\pm\tau^{0},\pm\mathrm{i}\tau^{1},\pm\mathrm{i}\tau^{2},\pm\mathrm{i}\tau^{3}\}, so the search for the sublattice matrices gO​(μ)g_{O}(\mu) can be restricted to this group without loss of generality. For each class the canonical form is the first solution in a fixed ordering of the sublattice matrices. The complete canonical forms, sign parameters and all sublattice matrices, of the PSGs of p​4​m​m×ℤ2Θp4mm\times\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{\Theta} and p​4​m​mp4mm, the latter being the algebraic PSGs of the chiral classes, are provided in the SM, together with the phase functions of the flux families, and the characters of the chiral classes. A chiral state labeled 𝒦\mathcal{K}:X has the PSG X of the space group alone, with the character of class 𝒦\mathcal{K}. The counting of the PSGs, Eq. (S3), and the canonical forms of the U⁡(1)U(1) PSGs and flux families are given in Sec. SII of the SM.

B.2 Chiral PSGs

For a chiral class the elements with ϵ⁡(g)=−1\epsilon(g)=-1 are combined with time reversal and act on the ansatz as u→−G​u​G†u\to-G\,u\,G^{\dagger}, with the spin rotation acting on the triplet components. This changes the conditions on the ansatz but not the algebra of the gauge matrices, so the algebraic PSGs of every chiral class are those of p​4​m​mp4mm alone: 4040 ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}, 2424 discrete U⁡(1)U(1) and one flux family, and 44 S​U​(2)SU(2) PSGs. The character enters the realization through the allowed amplitudes and on-site fields, and the canonical forms and labels of these PSGs are listed in the SM.

Appendix C Hierarchy of PSGs

The realized PSGs form a family tree. Adding new symmetry-allowed amplitudes to a state lowers its IGG while keeping all lattice symmetries: real hopping lowers S​U​(2)SU(2) to U⁡(1)U(1), and pairing lowers S​U​(2)SU(2) or U⁡(1)U(1) to ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}. The new state is a descendant of the old one, and its PSG is a subgroup of the parent PSG. Physically, parent and descendant are connected by a Higgs transition, in which a spinon hopping or pairing channel condenses.

The four S​U​(2)SU(2) states sit at the top of the tree. To lower one of them to U⁡(1)U(1), each generator must either keep or reverse a common τ3\tau^{3} axis, which gives one descendant in each of the 1616 sectors ww of Table 2. Lowering to ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} gives 5252 descendants per parent. Different parents can share descendants, so these numbers do not add up to totals. Every realized ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} PSG descends from a realized U⁡(1)U(1) or S​U​(2)SU(2) PSG, so no state in the classification stands alone.

Since all four S​U​(2)SU(2) parents have ζ=−\zeta=-, the tree starts from flat-band states with bonds only between square and bow-tie sites. Bonds within a site orbit, such as the square edge J1J_{1}, appear only further down the tree, in descendants in which time reversal no longer acts as a plain sign.

Appendix D Spin–Orbit Coupling: Moriya Rules and Symmetry Classes

D.1 Moriya Rules and Inverted Directions

For the classical Moriya rules of Sec. VIII.1 we assume a layer without the horizontal mirror z→−zz\to-z, as for buckled or supported layers in the materials. With this mirror every 𝑫\bm{D} would be along 𝒛^\hat{\bm{z}}, and 𝑫\bm{D} would vanish on the bonds whose stabilizer contains a twofold rotation. On the square-kagome lattice the rules give 𝑫\bm{D} in the plane of the perpendicular bisecting mirror on J1J_{1}, Jb​pJ_{bp}, and Jb​bJ_{bb}, in the plane on Jb​cJ_{bc}, only along the in-plane normal 𝒆^⟂\hat{\bm{e}}_{\perp} of the bond on JdJ_{d}, J×J_{\times}, Jb​sJ_{bs}, and J+J_{+}, whose stabilizers contain a twofold rotation and two mirrors, and no constraint on J23J_{23}, Js​bJ_{sb}, Jo​3J_{o3}, and JtJ_{t}.

Inverted directions arise on bonds where the PSG forbids the singlet hopping. In the U⁡(1)U(1) classes with wΘ=1w_{\Theta}=1, which are of Altland–Zirnbauer class AII (Appendix D.2), time reversal in the gauge GΘ=i​τ1G_{\Theta}=\mathrm{i}\tau^{1} keeps exactly the channels τ3\tau^{3} (singlet) and i​τ3\mathrm{i}\tau^{3} (triplet) on every bond, so that the triplet link is always parallel, in quaternion space, to the would-be singlet. Each stabilizer element gg of a bond multiplies this channel by a sign ϵ~g\tilde{\epsilon}_{g}, a character of the bond stabilizer. The singlet hopping is allowed exactly when ϵ~=1\tilde{\epsilon}=1 on the whole stabilizer, and the DM directions satisfy Rg​𝒏=ϵ~g​𝒏R_{g}\bm{n}=\tilde{\epsilon}_{g}\bm{n} for fixing and Rg​𝒏=−ϵ~g​𝒏R_{g}\bm{n}=-\tilde{\epsilon}_{g}\bm{n} for reversing elements, which gives the classical set for ϵ~=1\tilde{\epsilon}=1 and an inverted set otherwise. The characters follow in closed form from the relation values and the sector bits (Sec. SI of the SM): for instance ϵ~=(−1)wC4+wσ\tilde{\epsilon}=(-1)^{w_{C_{4}}+w_{\sigma}} on J1J_{1}, (−1)wT(-1)^{w_{T}} on Jb​cJ_{bc}, ηC4\eta_{C_{4}} for the twofold rotation about the square center on JdJ_{d} and Jb​sJ_{bs}, and ηC4​η12\eta_{C_{4}}\eta_{12} for the twofold rotation about the octagon center on J×J_{\times} and J+J_{+}.

The class U0001-0, projective only through ησ​T\eta_{\sigma T}, ηC4\eta_{C_{4}}, and ηΘ​T\eta_{\Theta T}, illustrates the mechanism. Its sign ηC4=−1\eta_{C_{4}}=-1 forbids the singlet hopping on JdJ_{d} and Jb​sJ_{bs}, and ηC4​η12=−1\eta_{C_{4}}\eta_{12}=-1 forbids it on J×J_{\times} and J+J_{+}. All four orbits carry instead an out-of-plane DM vector, 𝑫|𝒛^\bm{D}\parallel\hat{\bm{z}}, instead of 𝒆^⟂\hat{\bm{e}}_{\perp}. In classes in which wC4+wσw_{C_{4}}+w_{\sigma} is odd, such as U0011-nn and U0101-nn, the square edges carry no singlet hopping and a DM vector along the bond.

D.2 Altland–Zirnbauer Classes and Momentum Action

In the U⁡(1)U(1) classes with wΘ=0w_{\Theta}=0 time reversal acts as a unitary chiral operator on the Bloch Hamiltonian, class AIII, which in two dimensions has no strong invariant and forces C=C↑=0C=C_{\uparrow}=0. Every such PSG has an orbit-wise constant central GΘG_{\Theta} and either admits no amplitude or is a flat-band PSG, so that the statement is automatic. The S​U​(2)SU(2) PSGs are of class CII and trivial in two dimensions. Spinon quantum spin Hall states can therefore occur only in the AII classes among the U⁡(1)U(1) and S​U​(2)SU(2) PSGs, whereas ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} PSGs with spin–orbit coupling are of class DIII and are not surveyed. The twofold rotation C2=C42C_{2}=C_{4}^{2} conserves spinon number in every class. Time reversal maps 𝒌→−𝒌+(π,π)\bm{k}\to-\bm{k}+(\pi,\pi) in the classes with ηΘ​T=−1\eta_{\Theta T}=-1, and C2C_{2} maps 𝒌→−𝒌+(π,π)\bm{k}\to-\bm{k}+(\pi,\pi) when ηC4​T=−1\eta_{C_{4}T}=-1. The product C2​ΘC_{2}\Theta is therefore local in momentum only when the two shifts coincide, and then (C2​Θ)2=ηC4(C_{2}\Theta)^{2}=\eta_{C_{4}}. When the shifts differ, as in U0001-0, C2​ΘC_{2}\Theta maps 𝒌→𝒌+(π,π)\bm{k}\to\bm{k}+(\pi,\pi), and every band satisfies E⁡(𝒌)=E⁡(𝒌+(π,π))E(\bm{k})=E(\bm{k}+(\pi,\pi)). This gauge-invariant bulk property is the projective signature of such classes, whereas the momentum at which edge Kramers pairs cross depends on the gauge of the projective translation on a ribbon and carries no such information. In the staggered sectors the translation combined with time reversal is a chiral operator at every momentum, so that the spectrum is symmetric under E→−EE\to-E and EF=0E_{F}=0 is pinned.

The flat-band PSGs of Sec. IV.3 allow triplet amplitudes only on the square–bow-tie bonds, so that the Bloch matrix keeps the block form of Eq. (18) and at least four exact zero modes per momentum survive any PSG-allowed spin–orbit coupling. Where B⁡(𝒌)B(\bm{k}) has full rank at every momentum, the flat manifold is the orthogonal complement of the span of its columns and hence a trivial bundle with Chern number zero. Where dispersive bands touch the flat bands, as in SU000-000-000−- at MM, the flat manifold is not separated from them and carries no Chern number of its own. In all our spin–orbit-coupled samples of these PSGs the flat manifold is separated from the dispersive bands, by at least 0.130.13. In nine further U⁡(1)U(1) classes of p​4​m​mp4mm, U0011-0, U0011-2, U0101-0, U1001-0, U1011-0, U1011-3, U1101-0, U1111-0, and U1111-1, every ansatz up to J+J_{+}, with singlet, triplet, and on-site terms, has exact zero modes at a time-reversal-invariant momentum. The mechanism is a splitting of the levels there into sectors of odd dimension, each mapped onto itself by an antiunitary particle–hole operation, and it accounts for all zero modes except four of the twelve in U1011-0.

Appendix E Regular Magnetic Orders

In a regular order every element gg of p​4​m​mp4mm is undone by a global O⁡(3)O(3) operation RgR_{g}, and g↦Rgg\mapsto R_{g} is a homomorphism [72]. For magnetic cells of at most 2×22\times 2 unit cells, RgR_{g} factors through F=p​4​m​m/⟨T12,T22⟩F=p4mm/\langle T_{1}^{2},T_{2}^{2}\rangle, a group of order 3232 with fourteen real irreducible representations: A1A_{1}, A2A_{2}, B1B_{1}, B2B_{2}, EE (wave vector Γ\Gamma), M1M_{1}–M5M_{5} (MM), and X1X_{1}–X4X_{4} (XX and YY, induced from the little group 2​m​m2mm). A three-dimensional orthogonal representation of FF defines a family of regular orders through the spin of a reference site in each orbit, which must be fixed by the image of the site stabilizer. Of the 168168 three-dimensional representations, 8484 allow nonzero spins on both orbits. By wave-vector content, 1515 are at Γ\Gamma, 4545 at Γ\Gamma and MM, 1212 at Γ\Gamma and XX, 88 at MM and XX, and 44 at MM. Of the irreducible blocks, A1A_{1}, M5M_{5}, X1X_{1}, and X4X_{4} carry spins on both orbits, B1B_{1} on the bow-tie sites only, and B2B_{2}, EE, M1M_{1}, M4M_{4}, X2X_{2}, and X3X_{3} on the square sites only, while A2A_{2}, M2M_{2}, and M3M_{3} carry no spins. Grouping the representations by the space they span gives 4646 families: one collinear, containing the ferromagnet and the Lieb ferrimagnet, 1111 coplanar, and 3434 noncoplanar.

The energy per site of a family is a quadratic form in the amplitudes xx, yy of its blocks on the two orbits, E/N=∑(a​x2+b​y2−2​|c|​x​y)E/N=\sum(ax^{2}+by^{2}-2|c|xy), with coefficients linear in all twelve couplings, minimized over unit spin length on every site. For the orders of the cross-octagon model with J1=J2=J3=1J_{1}=J_{2}=J_{3}=1 this gives

E2​π/3\displaystyle E_{2\pi/3} =−1+13​(J++J×),\displaystyle=-1+\tfrac{1}{3}(J_{+}+J_{\times}),
Ecuboc1\displaystyle E_{\rm cuboc1} =−1−13​(J++J×),\displaystyle=-1-\tfrac{1}{3}(J_{+}+J_{\times}),
EB2+M5\displaystyle E_{B_{2}+M_{5}} =3+J×2+J+−J×​(J++3)3​(J×−1),\displaystyle=\frac{3+J_{\times}^{2}+J_{+}-J_{\times}(J_{+}+3)}{3(J_{\times}-1)},
E2​π/3​-d\displaystyle E_{2\pi/3\text{-d}} =−6+J×2−2​J+−J×​(J+−4)3​(J×+2),\displaystyle=-\frac{6+J_{\times}^{2}-2J_{+}-J_{\times}(J_{+}-4)}{3(J_{\times}+2)}, (32)

and for J1=J2=J3=−1J_{1}=J_{2}=J_{3}=-1 the ferromagnetic and octagonal energies EFM=−2+13​(J++J×)E_{\rm FM}=-2+\frac{1}{3}(J_{+}+J_{\times}) and Eoct=−13​(2+2​2+J++J×)E_{\rm oct}=-\frac{1}{3}(2+2\sqrt{2}+J_{+}+J_{\times}), in agreement with Ref. [26]. The energies of cuboc1 and cuboc-d′ (M4+M5M_{4}+M_{5}) coincide with that of B2+M5B_{2}+M_{5} on the line J×=0J_{\times}=0. The scalar chiralities of the cross-octagon orders are as follows. The nearest-neighbor triangles are coplanar in all of them. The chirality of cuboc1 is given in Sec. IX.2. In B2+M5B_{2}+M_{5} the chiralities alternate around each square with translation-invariant signs and a magnitude of 1/21/\sqrt{2} at J×=0J_{\times}=0 that decreases with |J×||J_{\times}|. In M4+M5M_{4}+M_{5} they have the same magnitude with a (π,π)(\pi,\pi) staggering, and in the conical order only loops around the octagons carry chirality, staggered in sign. None has a net chirality.

The 3434 noncoplanar families, with their blocks, chiral classes, and parent Hamiltonians, are provided in the SM. They distribute over the chiral classes as ℬ\mathcal{B} 66, 𝒞\mathcal{C} 44, 𝒟\mathcal{D} 44, 𝒜′\mathcal{A}^{\prime} 44, ℬ′\mathcal{B}^{\prime} 66, 𝒞′\mathcal{C}^{\prime} 44, and 𝒟′\mathcal{D}^{\prime} 66, and no family falls into class 𝒜\mathcal{A}. For each family we optimized the twelve couplings for the largest margin by which all other modes lie above the Luttinger–Tisza minimum, with one Lagrange multiplier per site orbit, and evaluated the bound on dense momentum grids including rings around the ordering wave vectors, and by annealing on 2×22\times 2, 4×44\times 4, and 8×88\times 8 tori and on twisted cells. Saturation of the generalized Luttinger–Tisza bound proves that the order is a classical ground state, and uniqueness means that every annealed state equals the order up to O⁡(3)O(3) and lattice symmetry.

Of the 1717 families with exact parent Hamiltonians and an open stability region in the space of the twelve couplings, 1313 have a unique ground state, and the three class-ℬ\mathcal{B} families among them are A1+M5A_{1}+M_{5}, M1+X4M_{1}+X_{4}, and M4+X1M_{4}+X_{1}. Within the couplings of Ref. [26] only the conical order has an exact parent with an open stability region (besides the C4C_{4}-breaking cuboc1 and cuboc3), and all other parents need further orbits. The noncoplanar member of the 2​π/32\pi/3-d family is exact with the additional coupling Js​bJ_{sb}, where it is degenerate with C4C_{4}-breaking members of the same family that harmonic fluctuations favor. Three families are exact only on a manifold of codimension one in coupling space: A1+B1+B2A_{1}+B_{1}+B_{2} and B1+M1+M4B_{1}+M_{1}+M_{4}, where the order is degenerate with coplanar members, and the twelve-direction cuboc-d order M4+M5M_{4}+M_{5}, which stays the unique ground state on the manifold J×+Jb​p−Jb​c=2​Jo​3​(J1−Jd−Jb​p+2​Jb​c−J×)/|J23−Js​b−Jo​3|J_{\times}+J_{bp}-J_{bc}=2J_{o3}(J_{1}-J_{d}-J_{bp}+2J_{bc}-J_{\times})/|J_{23}-J_{sb}-J_{o3}|. On this manifold the coupling between its two blocks that is linear in the momentum deviation vanishes. In the model of Ref. [26] the manifold reduces to the line J×=0J_{\times}=0, where M4+M5M_{4}+M_{5} is degenerate with B2+M5B_{2}+M_{5} and cuboc1. For the remaining families, which have no Luttinger–Tisza-saturating parent with couplings up to J+J_{+}, two kinds of obstruction appear: blocks at the same wave vector that couple linearly in the momentum deviation, which makes the LT minimum incommensurate, and degeneracies with coplanar members that hold on manifolds of codimension one or two.

Supplemental Material for “Melting noncoplanar order on the square-kagome lattice: Chiral, flat-band, and staggered spin liquids from projective symmetry”
Harsh Raj1, Atanu Maity2,1, and Yasir Iqbal1

1Department of Physics, Indian Institute of Technology Madras, Chennai 600036, India

This Supplemental Material (SM) collects derivations and method details that support the main text. The data files that accompany it [86] contain the canonical forms of all projective symmetry groups, the amplitudes, spectra, densities of states, and structure factors of all realized spin liquids, the representative chiral and spin–orbit-coupled states, the self-consistent PSG-manifold scans, the catalog of regular orders, and the projected energies.

Appendix SI Bond Orbits and Reference-Bond Amplitudes

Table S1 lists the twelve bond orbits up to the length 1+31+\sqrt{3} of J×J_{\times} and J+J_{+}, drawn in Fig. 1(b) and (c) of the main text, with their reference bonds and stabilizers. The orbits J23J_{23}, Js​bJ_{sb}, Jo​3J_{o3}, and JtJ_{t} have eight bonds per cell, as many as the order of the point group, so their bonds have trivial stabilizers. Several further-neighbor bonds close triangles with nearest-neighbor bonds: JdJ_{d} with two square edges, Jb​pJ_{bp} and Jb​bJ_{bb} with two bow-tie edges, and Js​bJ_{sb} with one edge of each kind. The bond Jb​cJ_{bc} is the straight diagonal of a bow-tie and closes no triangle. The next shell, at length (5+2​3)1/2(5+2\sqrt{3})^{1/2}, contains two further orbits at graph distance three, which are not included.

Once the amplitudes on the reference bond i→ji\to j of an orbit are fixed, Eq. (9) of the main text determines them on every other bond of the orbit. The reference amplitudes are restricted by the elements of p​4​m​mp4mm that map the unoriented bond onto itself and by time reversal. Two kinds of spatial element occur (Table S1). A reversing element O¯\bar{O}, with O¯​(i)=j\bar{O}(i)=j and O¯​(j)=i\bar{O}(j)=i, imposes

ui​j(0)†=GO¯(j)ui​j(0)GO¯†(i),u^{(0)\dagger}_{ij}=G_{\bar{O}}(j)\,u^{(0)}_{ij}\,G_{\bar{O}}^{\dagger}(i), (S1)

and a fixing element FF, with F⁡(i)=iF(i)=i and F⁡(j)=jF(j)=j, imposes

ui​j(0)=GF​(i)​ui​j(0)​GF†​(j),u^{(0)}_{ij}=G_{F}(i)\,u^{(0)}_{ij}\,G_{F}^{\dagger}(j), (S2)

together with the corresponding conditions on the triplet links, which carry the spin rotation RO¯R_{\bar{O}} or RFR_{F}. Fixing elements occur for JdJ_{d} and J×J_{\times} (the diagonal mirror σ\sigma), Jb​sJ_{bs} (the axial mirror σ​C4\sigma C_{4}), and J+J_{+} (the axial mirror T1​σ​C4−1T_{1}\sigma C_{4}^{-1} through the octagon center). Because the sublattice matrices of Eq. (15) of the main text are quaternions rather than signs, GO¯​(i)G_{\bar{O}}(i) and GF​(i)G_{F}(i) are in general not proportional to τ0\tau^{0}, and the conditions mix the channels of Eq. (7). The allowed singlet spaces are then not always spanned by basis matrices. In the data files of the SM such spaces are marked d∗d^{\ast}. Time reversal imposes Eq. (10) with GΘ​(i)=ηΘ​Tx+y​gΘ​(μi)G_{\Theta}(i)=\eta_{\Theta T}^{x+y}g_{\Theta}(\mu_{i}). For a central GΘG_{\Theta} it reduces to the selection rule of Sec. IV.2.

In a chiral class an element OO with ϵ⁡(O)=−1\epsilon(O)=-1 is combined with time reversal and imposes Eq. (S1) or (S2) with an additional minus sign, and the time-reversal condition is dropped. For the U⁡(1)U(1) PSGs the factors (i​τ1)wO(\mathrm{i}\tau^{1})^{w_{O}} of the transforming elements reverse the channel τ3\tau^{3} and leave i​τ0\mathrm{i}\tau^{0} unchanged, and for the S​U​(2)SU(2) PSGs only the channel i​τ0\mathrm{i}\tau^{0} remains. The allowed spaces, the common null spaces of all these linear conditions, were computed for every PSG and every orbit, with a fixed sign convention for their basis vectors. For the nearest-neighbor S​U​(2)SU(2) states the result is simple: a singlet amplitude i​χ​τ0\mathrm{i}\chi\tau^{0} is allowed on a bond only if it is odd under time reversal, hi​hj=−1h_{i}h_{j}=-1, which for the four realized S​U​(2)SU(2) PSGs selects the square–bow-tie orbits J23J_{23}, Js​bJ_{sb}, and Jo​3J_{o3}.

Triplet directions. The triplet links carry the spin rotation RgR_{g} of each stabilizer element, the axial-vector action of its rotation part, in which a mirror acts as the twofold rotation about its normal. In the AII classes (U⁡(1)U(1), wΘ=1w_{\Theta}=1) time reversal in the gauge GΘ=i​τ1G_{\Theta}=\mathrm{i}\tau^{1} keeps only the channels τ3\tau^{3} and i​τ3\mathrm{i}\tau^{3}, and each stabilizer element multiplies them by a common sign ϵ~g\tilde{\epsilon}_{g} (Sec. VIII.1). Table S2 lists, for the orbits of p​4​m​mp4mm with a nontrivial stabilizer, the classical DM directions, the closed forms of ϵ~\tilde{\epsilon} in terms of the relation values and sector bits, and the inverted directions. In every AII class ησ=(−1)wσ\eta_{\sigma}=(-1)^{w_{\sigma}}. The orbits J23J_{23}, Js​bJ_{sb}, Jo​3J_{o3}, and JtJ_{t} have trivial stabilizers and allow the singlet hopping and all three DM components in every AII class. In the U⁡(1)U(1) classes with wΘ=0w_{\Theta}=0 and in the flat-band PSGs, time reversal allows every channel on bonds with hi​hj=−1h_{i}h_{j}=-1 and none on bonds with hi​hj=+1h_{i}h_{j}=+1, so that the flat-band PSGs carry spin–orbit coupling only on J23J_{23}, Js​bJ_{sb}, and Jo​3J_{o3}.

Realization by range. Table S3 gives the number of realized PSGs of p​4​m​m×ℤ2Θp4mm\times\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{\Theta} as a function of the range of the ansatz (main text, Sec. V).

Appendix SII Counting and U⁡(1)U(1) Canonical Forms of the PSGs

This section completes the derivation of the projective symmetry groups outlined in Appendix B of the main text, whose canonical gauge and relation values, Eq. (15) of the main text, it uses.

A Counting

The ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} PSGs follow from the cohomology classes and the on-site representations of the site stabilizers. For the cohomology, the group acts freely on a set of points consisting of the general-position orbit of p​4​m​mp4mm and two copies of it exchanged by Θ\Theta. On such a set every cohomology class is realized by sign-valued gauge transformations, and eliminating the signs GO​(x)G_{O}(x) on a patch of (2​R+1)2(2R+1)^{2} cells over ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}, without gauge fixing, leaves the linear constraints on the thirteen relation values. Modulo re-liftings this is H2​(p​4​m​m×ℤ2Θ,ℤ2)=ℤ210H^{2}(p4mm\times\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{\Theta},\mathbb{Z}_{2})=\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{10}, stable for R=1R=1, 22, 33. Carrying along the relators of a presentation of each site stabilizer, written as words in the generators, expresses the extension of the stabilizer as a linear function of the class η\eta. For each class we enumerated the two-dimensional representations of the extended stabilizers that map the nontrivial element of the IGG to −τ0-\tau^{0}, in the dicyclic group of order 4848 and in the binary octahedral group, and identified them by their characters. For the elementary abelian stabilizers of the square-kagome lattice the quaternion group suffices. The binary octahedral group, which contains elements of order 88, is needed for the 1​a1a positions of the Lieb and square lattices compared in Sec. SIII, where C4C_{4} can be represented by ei​π​τ3/4e^{\mathrm{i}\pi\tau^{3}/4}. A PSG is a class together with one on-site representation per orbit, and the re-liftings, the characters of p​4​m​m×ℤ2Θp4mm\times\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{\Theta}, act on the representations of both orbits simultaneously. The number of PSGs is

N=∑η|(Rb​(η)×Rs​(η))/Hom⁡(p​4​m​m×ℤ2Θ,ℤ2)|,N=\sum_{\eta}\big|\big(R_{b}(\eta)\times R_{s}(\eta)\big)/\mathrm{Hom}(p4mm\times\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{\Theta},\mathbb{Z}_{2})\big|, (S3)

where Rb​(η)R_{b}(\eta) and Rs​(η)R_{s}(\eta) are the inequivalent on-site representations of the class on the bow-tie and square orbits. Because the twist is simultaneous, NN is not a product of single-orbit counts: the relative sign ζ\zeta of a central time-reversal matrix on the two orbits survives it. Equation (S3) gives the 200200 PSGs of p​4​m​m×ℤ2Θp4mm\times\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{\Theta}. Equivalently, the PSGs are the solutions of the PSG equations on a 2×22\times 2 torus, with the matrices GO​(i)G_{O}(i) of all generators on all sites and the thirteen relation values as unknowns, gauge-fixed only on a spanning tree of each orbit, reduced to their relation values and the traces of their on-site stabilizer matrices and taken modulo the re-lifting group. A depth-first search with constraint propagation enumerates them.

Independent check. The script check_psg_classification.py of the data files uses only the tabulated forms, the symmetry action, and the bond orbits. It reconstructs every PSG on a patch and confirms that all thirteen relations take the tabulated values on every site and that each GOG_{O} of a U⁡(1)U(1) PSG lies in its sector. For the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} PSGs, the relation values together with the traces of GhG_{h} at the fixed sites of the site stabilizers hh and of h​Θh\Theta are gauge invariant up to the sign changes Gg→−GgG_{g}\to-G_{g} of the generators. Minimized over these sign changes, they differ for all 200200 PSGs, which are therefore pairwise inequivalent. Finally, it computes the allowed singlet amplitudes of every PSG on all twelve orbits, builds a random ansatz on a patch, and obtains its IGG as the commutant of the links. This reproduces the realized PSGs, 160160, 5757, and 44 up to J+J_{+} and 4040, 2121, and 44 with nearest-neighbor bonds, with the same labels as the tables.

B U⁡(1)U(1) Canonical Forms

For the IGG U⁡(1)U(1) every PSG element has the form GO​(i)=ei​ϕO​(i)​τ3​(i​τ1)wOG_{O}(i)=e^{\mathrm{i}\phi_{O}(i)\tau^{3}}(\mathrm{i}\tau^{1})^{w_{O}}, and the sector ww is a character of p​4​m​m×ℤ2Θp4mm\times\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{\Theta}. In the staggered sectors, wT=1w_{T}=1, the gauge transformation W⁡(x,y)=(i​τ1)wT​(x+y)W(x,y)=(\mathrm{i}\tau^{1})^{w_{T}(x+y)}, an integer matrix power (not reduced mod 22), maps the translations to sign forms, and we write the canonical forms G′G^{\prime} in this gauge, in which the IGG is {ei​θ​(−1)wT​(x+y)​τ3}\{e^{\mathrm{i}\theta(-1)^{w_{T}(x+y)}\tau^{3}}\}. The PSG acting on the ansatz is GO​(i)=W​(i)−1​GO′​(i)​W​(O−1​i)G_{O}(i)=W(i)^{-1}G^{\prime}_{O}(i)\,W(O^{-1}i), with IGG {ei​θ​τ3}\{e^{\mathrm{i}\theta\tau^{3}}\}. All tabulated amplitudes and multipliers refer to this gauge. Within each sector the cohomology classes were computed by an exact integer elimination on a free set of sites, without on-site conditions, and the PSGs by an elimination on the sites of the square-kagome lattice that includes the on-site conditions of both orbits (Table 2 of the main text). The canonical forms are structured as in Eq. (15), with gO​(μ)g_{O}(\mu) in the normalizer of the IGG, diagonal for wO=0w_{O}=0 and off-diagonal for wO=1w_{O}=1. In particular, gC4​(μ)=i​τ1g_{C_{4}}(\mu)=\mathrm{i}\tau^{1} on the tree sublattices μ=2,3,4,6\mu=2,3,4,6 for wC4=1w_{C_{4}}=1. Two PSGs are counted as distinct if they differ in their relation values or in the gauge-invariant on-site values of the stabilizer elements with wO=0w_{O}=0, modulo re-liftings and the global transformation i​τ1\mathrm{i}\tau^{1}. In the sector (0,0,1,0)(0,0,1,0) the flux family takes the form

GT2​(x,y,μ)\displaystyle G_{T_{2}}(x,y,\mu) =ei​Φ​x​τ3,\displaystyle=e^{\mathrm{i}\Phi x\tau^{3}},
GC4​(x,y,μ)\displaystyle G_{C_{4}}(x,y,\mu) =ei​Φ​x​y​τ3​gC4​(μ),\displaystyle=e^{\mathrm{i}\Phi xy\tau^{3}}\,g_{C_{4}}(\mu),
Gσ​(x,y,μ)\displaystyle G_{\sigma}(x,y,\mu) =ei​Φ​x​y​τ3​gσ​(μ),\displaystyle=e^{\mathrm{i}\Phi xy\tau^{3}}\,g_{\sigma}(\mu), (S4)

with [T2,T1]=ei​Φ​τ3[T_{2},T_{1}]=e^{\mathrm{i}\Phi\tau^{3}}, while GT1=τ0G_{T_{1}}=\tau^{0} and GΘ​(x,y,μ)=ηΘ​Tx+y​gΘ​(μ)G_{\Theta}(x,y,\mu)=\eta_{\Theta T}^{x+y}g_{\Theta}(\mu) carry no Φ\Phi-dependent factor (the data files of the SM list the same phase functions Φ​x​y\Phi xy for GC4G_{C_{4}} and GσG_{\sigma} in all three flux families), and the sublattice matrices of the canonical form at Φ=0\Phi=0, in which gσ​(μ)∝i​τ1g_{\sigma}(\mu)\propto\mathrm{i}\tau^{1} reverses the U⁡(1)U(1) rotation. All relations are uniform elements of the IGG for every Φ\Phi, and Φ\Phi and −Φ-\Phi are identified by i​τ1\mathrm{i}\tau^{1}.

Appendix SIII PSGs of Other p​4​m​mp4mm Lattices

The square-kagome lattice is built from two simpler lattices with the same symmetry. The bow-tie sites alone form a checkerboard lattice (Wyckoff position 2​c2c), and the square sites alone form a lattice of squares on the diagonal mirror lines (4​d4d). The PSGs of these and other p​4​m​mp4mm lattices follow from the same 10241024 classes by the same on-site condition. Their counts are compared below.

A square-kagome PSG restricted to one site orbit gives a valid PSG of that sublattice, with the same class η\eta. Conversely, a checkerboard PSG cc and a square-site PSG dd combine into a square-kagome PSG exactly when they share the same class. When time reversal acts as a plain sign on both orbits, the relative sign ζ\zeta gives two ways to combine them:

PSGsqk\displaystyle\mathrm{PSG}_{\rm sqk} ={(c,d):η⁡(c)=η⁡(d)}\displaystyle=\{(c,d):\eta(c)=\eta(d)\}
×{ζ=±ifGΘacts as a sign on both orbits}.\displaystyle\quad\times\{\zeta=\pm\ \text{if}\ G_{\Theta}\ \text{acts as a sign on both orbits}\}. (S5)

Of the 240240 checkerboard and 640640 square-site PSGs, 160160 of each form matching pairs. 120120 pairs give one square-kagome PSG and 4040 give two, which reproduces the 200200 ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} PSGs of Sec. IV.1 of the main text. Similarly, the 88 S​U​(2)SU(2) PSGs come from 44 pairs with two choices of ζ\zeta each. The PSGs of a lattice with two site orbits are thus built from those of its sublattices, and are not simply the cohomology classes.

The construction of the main text applies to any p​4​m​mp4mm lattice: the PSGs follow from the cohomology classes of p​4​m​m×ℤ2Θp4mm\times\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{\Theta} through the on-site representations of the site stabilizers. Table S4 compares the counts for the single orbits of the square-kagome lattice and for other p​4​m​mp4mm lattices. For the square lattice the construction gives the 272272 ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} PSGs of Wen’s classification.

The square-site set is not the square-octagon lattice, whose vertices lie on the axial mirror lines, at 4​e4e or 4​f4f. No automorphism of p​4​m​mp4mm exchanges the two classes of mirrors. The two lattices have the same totals, because their on-site conditions differ only by the relabeling nσ↔nσ​C4n_{\sigma}\leftrightarrow n_{\sigma C_{4}} together with ηΘ​σ→ηΘ​σ​ηΘ​C4\eta_{\Theta\sigma}\to\eta_{\Theta\sigma}\eta_{\Theta C_{4}}, a bijection of the label space, while their U⁡(1)U(1) sector distributions are related by wσ→wσ+wC4w_{\sigma}\to w_{\sigma}+w_{C_{4}}. The square-octagon classification of Maity et al. cited in the main text fixes the on-site time-reversal matrix such that nearest-neighbor amplitudes are allowed: its 384384 ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} PSGs are exactly the classes of our 640640 with GΘ​(i)2=−1G_{\Theta}(i)^{2}=-1, and its 3232 S​U​(2)SU(2) PSGs are those of one of our four time-reversal sectors, the one in which GΘG_{\Theta} is the bipartite sign of the lattice. The four realized S​U​(2)SU(2) states are the same. Its U⁡(1)U(1) entries count the parameter choices of its canonical forms, a different counting rule, and we compare only the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} and S​U​(2)SU(2) counts.

Appendix SIV Spectra and Structure Factors

The ansätze of the spectral survey (main text, Sec. VII.3) contain singlet amplitudes on all orbits allowed by their PSG up to J+J_{+}, with the magnitudes stated there. On the reference bond of each orbit (Table S1) the link is u=|u|​𝒏^⋅(i​τ0,τ1,τ2,τ3)u=|u|\,\hat{\bm{n}}\cdot(\mathrm{i}\tau^{0},\tau^{1},\tau^{2},\tau^{3}) with 𝒏^\hat{\bm{n}} a fixed random unit vector in the allowed space, including its sign, since for a one-dimensional allowed space the sign selects a flux sector. The amplitudes on the other bonds follow from the PSG. U⁡(1)U(1) ansätze are written in the gauge in which the IGG is {ei​θ​τ3}\{e^{\mathrm{i}\theta\tau^{3}}\} (Sec. SII), and the flux families are taken at Φ=π/2\Phi=\pi/2. The multipliers allowed by the PSG are solved on both site orbits at half filling. The second amplitude point B uses independently drawn directions.

The reciprocal vectors of the Bravais lattice, Eq. (1) of the main text, are 𝒃1=(2​π/a)​(1,0)\bm{b}_{1}=(2\pi/a)(1,0) and 𝒃2=(2​π/a)​(0,1)\bm{b}_{2}=(2\pi/a)(0,1), and the first Brillouin zone (FBZ) is the square |kx|,|ky|≤π/a|k_{x}|,|k_{y}|\leq\pi/a. Its high-symmetry points are Γ=(0,0)\Gamma=(0,0), with little group 4​m​m4mm, X=(1/2,0)X=(1/2,0) and the equivalent Y=(0,1/2)Y=(0,1/2), with little group 2​m​m2mm, and M=(1/2,1/2)M=(1/2,1/2), with little group 4​m​m4mm, in units of 2​π/a2\pi/a. For PSGs with η12=−1\eta_{12}=-1 the ansatz is periodic on the doubled cell spanned by 𝑻1\bm{T}_{1} and 2​𝑻22\bm{T}_{2}, for the staggered U⁡(1)U(1) sectors on the cell spanned by 2​𝑻12\bm{T}_{1} and 2​𝑻22\bm{T}_{2}, and for the flux families at Φ=π/2\Phi=\pi/2 on a cell of four unit cells.

A state is classified as gapped if its indirect and direct gaps are nonzero, as having Fermi pockets if the bands overlap, and as having nodal lines if the direct gap vanishes along lines across the zone. Isolated nodes are classified by the powers of the gap along the principal axes of its quadratic form, linear in both directions for a Dirac node and quadratic in both for a quadratic band touching. Exactly flat bands at the Fermi level define a separate type. A count of the zero levels at all momenta, which also detects flat bands crossed by dispersive bands, finds such a level at every momentum in the 6969 states of Sec. IV.3 of the main text and in no other state at point A. Restricted to their nearest-neighbor amplitudes, with the directions of point A and self-consistent multipliers, 7878 further states have flat bands at EFE_{F}. Small closed nodal loops, such as those around Γ\Gamma and MM in Z000-101-111(1), count as nodal lines. For each Dirac state we count NfN_{f} as the number of two-component cones including spin. In states whose bands are twofold degenerate at every momentum a fourfold linear point counts as two cones. Quadratic band touchings in mixed states are listed separately and not counted in NfN_{f}. Where the cones are strongly anisotropic, the density of states is linear only below a crossover energy, and fitted density-of-states prefactors are not cone prefactors. For these states we quote velocities and crossover energies.

The spin structure factors depend on 𝒒\bm{q} through the phases ei​𝒒⋅(𝒓i−𝒓j)e^{\mathrm{i}\bm{q}\cdot(\bm{r}_{i}-\bm{r}_{j})}. A momentum 𝑮\bm{G} is a period of S⁡(𝒒)S(\bm{q}) for all correlations if and only if 𝑮⋅𝒅∈2​π​ℤ\bm{G}\cdot\bm{d}\in 2\pi\mathbb{Z} for every site difference 𝒅\bm{d}. In the ideal geometry the site coordinates lie in 12​ℤ​[3]\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{3}], and the site differences contain (1,0)(1,0), a square edge, and (3,0)=𝑻1−(1,0)(\sqrt{3},0)=\bm{T}_{1}-(1,0). They generate a group of rank four, which is dense in the plane, so that S⁡(𝒒)S(\bm{q}) has no period other than 𝑮=0\bm{G}=0. It is nevertheless defined at every momentum, and we compute it with the ideal positions throughout.

As a display window [Fig. S1(f)] we use the extended Brillouin zone of a commensurate realization of the same bond graph. Placing the square sites at (±1,±1)(\pm 1,\pm 1) and the bow-tie sites at (3,0)(3,0) and (0,3)(0,3), in units of a fine square lattice, with lattice constant 66, keeps the nearest-neighbor graph and the group p​4​m​mp4mm, makes all site differences integer vectors of the fine lattice, and distorts the bonds by 12%12\% (bow-tie edges 5\sqrt{5}, square edges 22). Its extended zone is the square |qx|,|qy|≤3×2​π/a|q_{x}|,|q_{y}|\leq 3\times 2\pi/a, six times larger than the FBZ in linear size, with the points X′=6​X=(3,0)X^{\prime}=6X=(3,0) and M′=6​M=(3,3)M^{\prime}=6M=(3,3) in units of 2​π/a2\pi/a. A realization with square sites at (±3,±3)(\pm 3,\pm 3) and bow-tie sites at (8,0)(8,0), (0,8)(0,8) distorts the bonds by only 3%3\%, at the price of an extended zone with 128128 times the area of the FBZ. In the ideal geometry the window |qx,y|≤3|q_{x,y}|\leq 3 is not a period cell.

For an ansatz with singlet amplitudes only, the mean-field Hamiltonian conserves the number of the fermions Ψi​1=fi↑\Psi_{i1}=f_{i\uparrow} and Ψi​2=fi↓†\Psi_{i2}=f^{\dagger}_{i\downarrow}. Indeed, singlet hopping fi↑†​fj↑+fi↓†​fj↓=Ψi​1†​Ψj​1−Ψj​2†​Ψi​2f^{\dagger}_{i\uparrow}f_{j\uparrow}+f^{\dagger}_{i\downarrow}f_{j\downarrow}=\Psi^{\dagger}_{i1}\Psi_{j1}-\Psi^{\dagger}_{j2}\Psi_{i2} and singlet pairing fi↑†​fj↓†=Ψi​1†​Ψj​2f^{\dagger}_{i\uparrow}f^{\dagger}_{j\downarrow}=\Psi^{\dagger}_{i1}\Psi_{j2} are both of the form Ψ†​Ψ\Psi^{\dagger}\Psi, so that

HMF=∑i,jΨi†​Mi​j​Ψj,H_{\rm MF}=\sum_{i,j}\Psi_{i}^{\dagger}M_{ij}\Psi_{j}, (S6)

with a Hermitian 2​N×2​N2N\times 2N matrix MM. Because Ψi†​Ψi=ni↑−ni↓+1\Psi_{i}^{\dagger}\Psi_{i}=n_{i\uparrow}-n_{i\downarrow}+1, the spin component along zz is Siz=12​(Ψi†​Ψi−1)S^{z}_{i}=\frac{1}{2}(\Psi^{\dagger}_{i}\Psi_{i}-1), and its Fourier transform with the site positions 𝒓i\bm{r}_{i} of the ideal lattice is, for 𝒒≠0\bm{q}\neq 0,

Sz𝒒=∑ie−i𝒒⋅𝒓iSzi=12∑𝒌∑μΨ†𝒌,μΨ𝒌+𝒒,μ,S^{z}_{\bm{q}}=\sum_{i}e^{-\mathrm{i}\bm{q}\cdot\bm{r}_{i}}S^{z}_{i}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\bm{k}}\sum_{\mu}\Psi^{\dagger}_{\bm{k},\mu}\Psi_{\bm{k}+\bm{q},\mu}, (S7)

where Ψ𝒌,μ=Nc−1/2∑𝑹e−i𝒌⋅(𝑹+𝒅μ)Ψ𝑹,μ\Psi_{\bm{k},\mu}=N_{c}^{-1/2}\sum_{\bm{R}}e^{-\mathrm{i}\bm{k}\cdot(\bm{R}+\bm{d}_{\mu})}\Psi_{\bm{R},\mu} is defined with the phase of the actual site position (atomic gauge) and NcN_{c} is the number of unit cells. In this gauge the Bloch matrix M⁡(𝒌)M(\bm{k}) is not periodic in the reciprocal lattice, but the operator S𝒒zS^{z}_{\bm{q}} contains no form factors, and the expressions below hold at every momentum 𝒒\bm{q}, not only in the first Brillouin zone. The structure factor is therefore defined at every 𝒒\bm{q}. It is periodic only under those reciprocal vectors 𝑮\bm{G} with 𝑮⋅(𝒓i−𝒓j)∈2​π​ℤ\bm{G}\cdot(\bm{r}_{i}-\bm{r}_{j})\in 2\pi\mathbb{Z} for all pairs of sites, of which the ideal geometry has none besides 𝑮=0\bm{G}=0 (see above).

Let vn​(𝒌)v_{n}(\bm{k}) and En​(𝒌)E_{n}(\bm{k}) be the eigenvectors and eigenvalues of M⁡(𝒌)M(\bm{k}). The mean-field ground state fills all states with En​(𝒌)<0E_{n}(\bm{k})<0, and S𝒒zS^{z}_{\bm{q}} creates a particle-hole pair. Inserting a complete set of states in Sz​z​(𝒒,ω)=N−1​∑f|⟨f|S𝒒z|0⟩|2​δ​(ω−Ef+E0)S^{zz}(\bm{q},\omega)=N^{-1}\sum_{f}|\langle f|S^{z}_{\bm{q}}|0\rangle|^{2}\delta(\omega-E_{f}+E_{0}) gives

Sz​z(𝒒,ω)=14​N∑𝒌∑a,b′\displaystyle S^{zz}(\bm{q},\omega)=\frac{1}{4N}\sum_{\bm{k}}{\sum_{a,b}}^{\prime} |vb†​(𝒌)​va​(𝒌+𝒒)|2\displaystyle\left|v_{b}^{\dagger}(\bm{k})\,v_{a}(\bm{k}+\bm{q})\right|^{2}
×δ⁡(ω−Eb​(𝒌)+Ea​(𝒌+𝒒)),\displaystyle\times\delta\big(\omega-E_{b}(\bm{k})+E_{a}(\bm{k}+\bm{q})\big), (S8)

where the primed sum runs over occupied states aa with Ea​(𝒌+𝒒)<0E_{a}(\bm{k}+\bm{q})<0 and empty states bb with Eb​(𝒌)>0E_{b}(\bm{k})>0, and N=6​NcN=6N_{c} is the number of sites. The overlaps contain the full coherence factors of the Bogoliubov quasiparticles of the original fermions, so Eq. (S8) applies to ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} as well as to U⁡(1)U(1) and S​U​(2)SU(2) ansätze. Spin-rotation symmetry gives Sx​x=Sy​y=Sz​zS^{xx}=S^{yy}=S^{zz}, and we plot Sz​z​(𝒒,ω)S^{zz}(\bm{q},\omega) and its frequency integral Sz​z​(𝒒)S^{zz}(\bm{q}). The trace over the spin components is three times larger. Its average over large momentum regions is the on-site value N−1​∑i⟨(Siz)2⟩MFN^{-1}\sum_{i}\langle(S^{z}_{i})^{2}\rangle_{\rm MF}. With the 2×22\times 2 density matrix ρi\rho_{i} of Ψi\Psi_{i}, Wick’s theorem gives ⟨(Siz)2⟩MF=14​Tr​[ρi​(1−ρi)]=18−18​|𝒕i|2\langle(S^{z}_{i})^{2}\rangle_{\rm MF}=\frac{1}{4}\mathrm{Tr}[\rho_{i}(1-\rho_{i})]=\frac{1}{8}-\frac{1}{8}|\bm{t}_{i}|^{2}, where tik=⟨Ψi†​τk​Ψi⟩t^{k}_{i}=\langle\Psi^{\dagger}_{i}\tau^{k}\Psi_{i}\rangle are the deviations from the on-site constraints and Tr​ρi=1\mathrm{Tr}\,\rho_{i}=1 by spin-rotation symmetry. The value 1/81/8, half the value 1/41/4 of the physical spin because the mean-field state is singly occupied only with probability 1/21/2, therefore holds when the constraints are satisfied on every site. For ansätze with triplet amplitudes the number of Ψ\Psi fermions is not conserved, and the same calculation is carried out with the four-component Nambu spinor (fi↑,fi↓,fi↑†,fi↓†)(f_{i\uparrow},f_{i\downarrow},f^{\dagger}_{i\uparrow},f^{\dagger}_{i\downarrow}), which yields the full tensor Sa​b​(𝒒,ω)S^{ab}(\bm{q},\omega).

Flat-band states. The flat-band states are evaluated in the limit T→0+T\to 0^{+} of the grand-canonical ensemble. Their zero modes are then maximally mixed: the one-body density matrix is ρ=12​(1−sgn⁡h)\rho=\frac{1}{2}(1-\operatorname{sgn}h) with sgn⁡0=0\operatorname{sgn}0=0, and because hh of Eq. (18) of the main text is off-diagonal between the orbits, so is sgn⁡h\operatorname{sgn}h, and correlations between distinct sites of the same orbit vanish. Hence S⁡(𝒒)=18+2N​∑i,jcos⁡[𝒒⋅(𝒓i−𝒓j)]​⟨Siz​Sjz⟩S(\bm{q})=\frac{1}{8}+\frac{2}{N}\sum_{i,j}\cos[\bm{q}\cdot(\bm{r}_{i}-\bm{r}_{j})]\,\langle S^{z}_{i}S^{z}_{j}\rangle, with ii on the square and jj on the bow-tie sites. The fourfold rotation, which exchanges the two bow-tie sites of a cell and permutes the square sites, gives S⁡(X′)=1/8S(X^{\prime})=1/8. The two half-filled zero modes per spin and cell give S⁡(Γ)=1/24S(\Gamma)=1/24 and the elastic weight S0​(𝒒)≤S0​(Γ)=1/24S_{0}(\bm{q})\leq S_{0}(\Gamma)=1/24, and together with the fourfold rotation S⁡(M′)S(M^{\prime}). These values, S⁡(M′)=16+124​cos⁡[6​π/(1+3)]≈0.2007S(M^{\prime})=\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{24}\cos[6\pi/(1+\sqrt{3})]\approx 0.2007 among them, do not depend on the amplitudes. Where dispersive bands touch the flat bands, they hold up to small mesh effects. These values are properties of the grand-canonical T→0+T\to 0^{+} ensemble, which is not a total-spin singlet and has total-spin fluctuations. A state at fixed particle number or a projected state would give other values of S⁡(Γ)S(\Gamma), S0S_{0}, and S⁡(M′)S(M^{\prime}). In gapless states without flat bands, zero levels that fall on mesh points give a small weight at Γ\Gamma and at ω=0\omega=0 that decreases with the mesh and is not a property of the states.

Representative states. Figure S1 shows Sz​z​(𝒒)S^{zz}(\bm{q}) at point A for one state of each spectral type, the state whose maximum lies closest to the median of its type, together with the display window. The maps of all 221221 states are in the data files of the SM. Two properties hold in every state. First, the static weight per spin component averages to 1/81/8 (see above). Second, S⁡(𝒒,ω)=S⁡(−𝒒,ω)S(\bm{q},\omega)=S(-\bm{q},\omega), chiral states included, because the twofold rotation about the square center maps 𝒒→−𝒒\bm{q}\to-\bm{q} and is unitary in every chiral class (main text, Sec. VI.2). On the square-hexagon-dodecagon lattice some chiral classes show an asymmetry instead [85]. The 6969 flat-band states have the amplitude-independent values derived above, with the maximum S⁡(M′)≈0.2007S(M^{\prime})\approx 0.2007 in 6565 of them. In the other 152152 states the maximum lies between 0.1450.145 and 0.1890.189, inside the window in 139139 of them, and its range is nearly the same for all spectral types: 0.1450.145 to 0.1800.180 for the gapped states, 0.1500.150 to 0.1890.189 for the Dirac states, 0.1520.152 to 0.1830.183 for the states with nodal lines, and 0.1520.152 to 0.1800.180 for those with Fermi pockets. The static structure factor alone therefore does not distinguish the spectral types.

Appendix SV Spin–Orbit Coupling: Survey and Representative States

This section gives the survey of the 3232 AII classes and the representative spinon quantum spin Hall states of Sec. VIII.2 of the main text. The symmetry classes are given in Appendix D there.

In the AII classes with η12=−1\eta_{12}=-1, three spinons per primitive cell in a gapped band set require an even C↑C_{\uparrow}. In U0001-0 and U0001-2 the parity of C↑C_{\uparrow} equals the product ξ\xi of the C2C_{2} eigenvalues of the occupied spin-up bands at the time-reversal-invariant momenta [21], so that a singlet parent with ξ=−1\xi=-1 is gapless. The charge-conjugation theorem says nothing about spin–orbit coupling that breaks SzS^{z} conservation.

We surveyed all 3232 AII classes. For each class, singlet parents with amplitudes on all allowed orbits up to J+J_{+} were combined with random triplet amplitudes, either the SzS^{z}-conserving out-of-plane part or the full allowed space, of two strengths, with the multipliers fixed by ⟨ni⟩=1\langle n_{i}\rangle=1. The survey comprises 12801280 samples with SzS^{z}-conserving and 12801280 with generic spin–orbit coupling. Gaps were determined by separate refinement of the band extrema, minima of the direct gap, and line scans through all special points, and ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} invariants from the Wannier-center flow [101] and with the Fukui–Hatsugai method [25]. In classes with ηΘ​T=−1\eta_{\Theta T}=-1 time reversal maps 𝒌→−𝒌+(π,π)\bm{k}\to-\bm{k}+(\pi,\pi) in the gauge of the tabulated forms, and both methods are evaluated in the zone shifted by (π/2,π/2)(\pi/2,\pi/2). Edge modes are counted from levels localized on one edge, and gaps are also evaluated along the shifted time-reversal-invariant lines and at generic points. For SzS^{z}-conserving samples the spin Chern number C↑C_{\uparrow} is computed as well, and (−1)C↑=ξ(-1)^{C_{\uparrow}}=\xi holds in all 2525 gapped SzS^{z}-conserving samples of the classes where it applies. Of the SzS^{z}-conserving samples, 120120 are gapped and 2121 of them are ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}-odd, all in U0001-0 and U0001-2, as the charge-conjugation theorem requires. Of the samples with generic spin–orbit coupling, 4343 are gapped and 99 are ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}-odd. A further survey of 13201320 samples with generic spin–orbit coupling in the staggered and particle–hole-mirror classes found 1111 gapped states, all ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}-odd, in U1001-1, U1001-2, U1011-2, U1101-2, and U1101-3. In the non-staggered particle–hole classes an extended survey of 684684 samples, with all orbits up to J+J_{+}, all allowed multipliers, and two prescriptions for the singlet parents, found 3636 gapped states and one ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}-odd state, P1 in U0111-2, with single-spinon gap Δ=0.067\Delta=0.067 (band gap 0.1340.134) and one helical pair per edge on ribbons along 𝑻1\bm{T}_{1} and 𝑻1+𝑻2\bm{T}_{1}+\bm{T}_{2}. Such states are rare in our samples, and the absence of ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}-odd samples in the other non-staggered particle–hole classes is a sampled observation, not an exclusion. With conserved SzS^{z} the charge-conjugation theorem excludes them analytically. The absence of gapped samples in U0011-1, U0011-3, U0101-1, U0101-2, U0101-3, U1001-3, U1011-1, U1101-1, U1111-2, and U1111-3 is likewise a sampled observation, not an exclusion. Only the nine classes with forced zero modes and the flat-band PSGs are excluded analytically.

Table S5 lists the representative states of Fig. 5 of the main text and further examples. The singlet parent of Q1 has zero-energy lines k1=0k_{1}=0 and k2=0k_{2}=0 through the touching and ξ=−1\xi=-1, and a DM amplitude on the bow-tie edges alone does not open the touching. Ribbons along 𝑻1\bm{T}_{1} and 𝑻1+𝑻2\bm{T}_{1}+\bm{T}_{2} carry one helical pair per edge. The parent of Q2 has band touchings at XX and YY. Both states remain gapped with ℤ2=1\mathbb{Z}_{2}=1 when random spin–orbit amplitudes of size 0.10.1 on all orbits up to J+J_{+} are added. Random searches with all orbits up to J+J_{+} find spin Chern numbers of magnitude 22 and 33 in addition to 11. The states with C↑=±2C_{\uparrow}=\pm 2 are ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}-trivial, and their two helical pairs per edge are protected only by SzS^{z} conservation, whereas those with C↑=±3C_{\uparrow}=\pm 3 have three pairs per edge on both terminations.

In the staggered gauge sector U1101-3 of S1 the element C2​ΘC_{2}\Theta is not local in momentum, and we have not derived the origin of the twofold degeneracy, which all staggered sectors Uww-3 share. On a ribbon along 2​𝑻12\bm{T}_{1}, levels localized on one edge cross reference energies inside the gap an odd number of times between the two Kramers points, the criterion for one helical pair [48, 22]. The crossing momentum depends on the gauge chosen for the ribbon translation. The state S2 of U1011-2 has the largest gap among the staggered-sector samples and the same edge structure on both supercell terminations. The free-spinon spin thermal Hall conductivity (κx​y↑−κx​y↓)/2(\kappa^{\uparrow}_{xy}-\kappa^{\downarrow}_{xy})/2 of the states with conserved SzS^{z} approaches −C↑-C_{\uparrow} in units of π​kB2/(6​ℏ)\pi k_{B}^{2}/(6\hbar) well below the gap, as a mean-field property.

Appendix SVI Parameters of the States in the Figures of the Main Text

Flux states. The states of Figs. 3(e)–(g) and 4(a)–(d) of the main text have nearest-neighbor hopping ti​j=ei​θi​jt_{ij}=e^{\mathrm{i}\theta_{ij}} on the four square edges and eight bow-tie edges of each cell, translation invariant, with ti​jt_{ij} the coefficient of fi↑†​fj↑f^{\dagger}_{i\uparrow}f_{j\uparrow} (and of fi↓†​fj↓f^{\dagger}_{i\downarrow}f_{j\downarrow}). The phases θi​j\theta_{ij} are the least-squares solution of the linear equations that fix the counterclockwise fluxes of the six faces of a cell. The face fluxes of a cell must add to zero modulo 2​π2\pi, and we lift them accordingly (for the class-ℬ\mathcal{B} state ℬ\mathcal{B}:SU011-001 4×π/2+π−3​π=04\times\pi/2+\pi-3\pi=0). The spectrum depends only on the fluxes. With these conventions the (π/2,π/2,π)(\pi/2,\pi/2,\pi) state has the band gap 4−2​24-2\sqrt{2} (Δ=2−2\Delta=2-\sqrt{2}) and C=−1C=-1 per spin, the (π,0,π)(\pi,0,\pi) state the band gap 2​(3−1)2(\sqrt{3}-1) (Δ=3−1\Delta=\sqrt{3}-1), and the (0,0,π)(0,0,\pi) state Dirac nodes at the Fermi energy 1−31-\sqrt{3}. Chern numbers are computed with the Fukui–Hatsugai–Suzuki link variables. The plaquette angle sum is multiplied by −1/2π-1/2\pi to give C=(2​π)−1​∫FC=(2\pi)^{-1}\int F with the orientation kx→kyk_{x}\to k_{y}, the sign of Sec. VI.3.

Ribbon. The ribbon of Fig. 3(f) contains 3030 unit cells along 𝑻2\bm{T}_{2}, all six sites of each cell, and the bonds within it. It is periodic along 𝑻1\bm{T}_{1}. A state is assigned to an edge when more than half of its weight lies within 0.10.1 of the ribbon width from that edge.

Thermal Hall conductivity. The curve of Fig. 3(g) is Eq. (21) evaluated with the Kubo Berry curvature.

Self-consistent states. The self-consistent states of Sec. IX.4 were obtained with exact on-site constraints in the limit T→0+T\to 0^{+}, and gapless states at a small Fermi smearing. The structure factors of Fig. S2 include a small Gaussian broadening.

Appendix SVII Classical Modulated and Spiral States

The long-wavelength modulations of the regular orders of phases II and VII (main text, Sec. IX.1) lie below them by 2.2×10−42.2\times 10^{-4} per site at (J+,J×)=(0.6,−0.02)(J_{+},J_{\times})=(0.6,-0.02), 1.3×10−31.3\times 10^{-3} at (0.6,−0.05)(0.6,-0.05), and 1.5×10−41.5\times 10^{-4} at (−1,0.1)(-1,0.1), with a period of 9898, 4242, and 3535 unit cells, respectively. These energies are obtained on twisted Hermite-normal-form supercells and are therefore upper bounds. They lie within 10−510^{-5}–10−410^{-4} of the generalized Luttinger–Tisza bound evaluated with refined wave vectors, whose minimum lies at |δ​𝒒|∼10−2|\delta\bm{q}|\sim 10^{-2}. The modulation period times |J×||J_{\times}| is 1.91.9 to 2.12.1 at J+=0.6J_{+}=0.6 for |J×|=0.005|J_{\times}|=0.005, 0.020.02, and 0.050.05 (periods of about 380380, 9898, and 4242 cells), consistent with a period proportional to 1/|J×|1/|J_{\times}|. A Bloch-Hessian analysis of the regular orders shows that the 1212-direction order cuboc-d′ at (0.6,−0.05)(0.6,-0.05) and the coplanar 2​π/32\pi/3-d at (−1,0.1)(-1,0.1) have negative eigenvalues at small wave vectors, so that they are saddle points, whereas cuboc-d is a local minimum at (0.6,−0.05)(0.6,-0.05) that the modulated state undercuts only globally. For the spiral phases we have not computed the Hessian and show only that lower states exist. In phase III, for example, the energy at (J+,J×)=(1,−0.2)(J_{+},J_{\times})=(1,-0.2) is −1.35403-1.35403 per site, below the value −1.34515-1.34515 of the 12×1212\times 12 approximant, with a modulation period of 22.622.6 cells.

Two details of the cross-octagon study of Gembé et al. cited in the main text were compared with our calculations. The energy quoted there for phase IV agrees with our value at (J+,J×)=(0.2,−0.2)(J_{+},J_{\times})=(0.2,-0.2). The point (−0.2,−0.2)(-0.2,-0.2) given with it lies in the 2​π/32\pi/3 phase. The magnetization formula numbered 16 there gives imaginary values at some points of the conical phase as printed, and real values at these points with the radicand of the formula numbered 15.

Appendix SVIII Self-Consistent Solutions

For the self-consistent solutions of Sec. IX.4 of the main text, in each PSG manifold the minimum of ⟨H⟩\langle H\rangle within the manifold and the fixed point of the self-consistency map projected onto the manifold were computed. Symmetries were identified from gauge-invariant loop operators. The decoupled state lies in 224224 of the 955955 PSG manifolds of p​4​m​mp4mm, its chiral classes, and the nematic class: in those that allow a π\pi-flux J1J_{1} square and J+J_{+} amplitudes on both chain families.

Competing states. The lowest TRS states with a connected bond graph have bond IGG ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} at A0, C1a, and C1b and U⁡(1)U(1) at C1c and C1d, with energies −0.148099-0.148099 (A0), −0.149019-0.149019 (C1a), −0.146657-0.146657 (C1b), −0.147092-0.147092 (C1c), and −0.149527-0.149527 (C1d). At C1b any gap is below 10−310^{-3}. The lowest class-𝒟\mathcal{D} state at C1b, at −0.144515-0.144515, is gapped with single-spinon gap 0.02650.0265, has C=0C=0, and breaks time reversal only weakly, with a chirality of 9×10−49\times 10^{-4} on square triples. A gapless class-𝒞′\mathcal{C}^{\prime} state, in the PSG 𝒞′\mathcal{C}^{\prime}:U100-1, lies at −0.143691-0.143691. In the nematic class of cuboc1, a gapless state at C1a, at −0.143359-0.143359, breaks time reversal only on loops through the J+J_{+} and J×J_{\times} chords, with zero chirality on the nearest-neighbor triangles and on square triples, whereas the lowest state in the nematic manifolds at C1a, at −0.148814-0.148814, is TRS, breaks the fourfold rotation, and is nearly decoupled. Self-consistent class-𝒟′\mathcal{D}^{\prime} states exist at C1a (−0.1289-0.1289) and C1d (−0.1414-0.1414). They are gapless, and time reversal is broken only on loops through the J×J_{\times} and J+J_{+} bonds. Further self-consistent time-reversal-symmetric states include the fully symmetric gapped U⁡(1)U(1) state at −0.142434-0.142434, with no J+J_{+} or J×J_{\times} amplitude, which is the nearest-neighbor (π,0,π)(\pi,0,\pi) flux state with the on-site constraints imposed exactly (without them its Wick energy is −0.1531-0.1531, but its bow-tie densities are unequal, as discussed in Sec. VII.2 of the main text), and, at C1d, a symmetric state at −0.145852-0.145852 with single-spinon gap 0.06120.0612, half its band gap 0.12250.1225.

Structure factors of the class-ℬ\mathcal{B} state. Figure S2 shows the static and dynamical structure factors of the class-ℬ\mathcal{B} state ℬ\mathcal{B}:SU011-001 at C1b, computed from the mean-field two-spinon bubble, Eq. (S8). The maxima of Sz​z​(𝒒)S^{zz}(\bm{q}) pass close to the Bragg peaks of cuboc1, so that the static structure factor alone cannot distinguish the chiral liquid from short-range cuboc1 correlations (main text, Sec. IX.4). The two-spinon continuum starts at 2​Δℬ2\Delta_{\mathcal{B}}.

Projected energies at the nearest-neighbor point. In the study of Astrakhantsev et al. cited in the main text, the projected energy of the chiral state (π/2,π/2,π)(\pi/2,\pi/2,\pi), −0.40489​(3)​J1-0.40489(3)J_{1} per site on a 9696-site cluster, lies above those of the (0,0,0)(0,0,0) spinon Fermi-surface state (−0.42714​(2)​J1-0.42714(2)J_{1}), the (0,0,π)(0,0,\pi) Dirac state (−0.41720​(3)​J1-0.41720(3)J_{1}), the (π,0,π)(\pi,0,\pi) state (−0.41362​(3)​J1-0.41362(3)J_{1}), and the pinwheel and loop-six valence-bond crystals (−0.43333​(1)​J1-0.43333(1)J_{1} and −0.43009​(1)​J1-0.43009(1)J_{1}).

Appendix SIX Projected Wave Functions: Methods and Data

Clusters and wave functions. The projected states of Sec. IX.5 of the main text are computed on L×LL\times L unit cells, N=6​L2N=6L^{2} sites with L=4L=4, 66, 88, and 1010, with periodic boundary conditions for the spins. Number-conserving states (the U⁡(1)U(1) and S​U​(2)SU(2) states and the crystal) and the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} states are written as determinants in the basis (ci↑,ci↓†)(c_{i\uparrow},c^{\dagger}_{i\downarrow}). The cuboc1-ordered state, whose field mixes the spin components, uses a determinant without SzS^{z} conservation, sampled with exchanges and single and pair spin flips. The ordered state is the hopping ansatz with zero flux on the nearest-neighbor bonds, square hopping 11, bow-tie hopping rr, hoppings t×t_{\times} and t+t_{+} on the cross-octagon bonds, and the field hh along the classical cuboc1 directions. Table S6 lists the free parameters of each state. One amplitude of each PSG state fixes the normalization.

Boundary twists. The spinons are given boundary twists, while the spin Hamiltonian stays periodic. Number-conserving states are averaged over the 4×44\times 4 grid of complex charge twists θ1,2=2​π​(k+12)/4\theta_{1,2}=2\pi(k+\tfrac{1}{2})/4. For ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} states a complex twist is not a consistent boundary condition, since a pairing term changes with the choice of the wrapped end of the bond, and they are averaged over the four real twists. Twists with an open mean-field shell are skipped. The energies of every state per cluster and per twist are given in the data files of the SM. The ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} states depend strongly on the twist at C1b, by up to 0.0680.068 per site on 9696 sites and up to 0.050.05 on the larger clusters. With the best twist instead of the average, the TRS ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} state lies 0.0280.028 above the twist-averaged ordered state on 384384 sites, and the state N:Z00000-101 lies 0.0150.015 and 0.0200.020 above it on 384384 and 600600 sites, so that the ranking at C1b does not depend on the averaging.

Optimization and measurement. The parameters are optimized by stochastic reconfiguration with the twist cycled through its set, so that the parameters are twist averaged, in chunks of 1010 steps at one twist with 200200, 200200, 120120, and 8080 sweeps per step for L=4L=4, 66, 88, and 1010, until the energy drift between the two halves of the last 1616 chunks falls below three standard deviations. The ordered state is optimized by the second code with four twists per step, 4040, 2525, 1515, and 88 steps for L=4L=4 to 1010, each LL starting from the optimum at L−2L-2. Energies are measured at all twists, for the states of the first code with 40004000, 25002500, 16001600, and 10001000 sweeps per twist, together with all correlations ⟨𝑺i⋅𝑺j⟩\langle\bm{S}_{i}\cdot\bm{S}_{j}\rangle. The order parameter is m2=∑i≠j⟨𝑺i⋅𝑺j⟩​𝒏i⋅𝒏j/∑i≠j(𝒏i⋅𝒏j)2m^{2}=\sum_{i\neq j}\langle\bm{S}_{i}\cdot\bm{S}_{j}\rangle\,\bm{n}_{i}\cdot\bm{n}_{j}/\sum_{i\neq j}(\bm{n}_{i}\cdot\bm{n}_{j})^{2}, equal to 1/41/4 for the classical cuboc1 order of spins 1/21/2.

Checks. The two codes agree to 10−710^{-7} in exact enumeration of projected states on 2424 sites, and their twist-averaged energies agree within 1.51.5 standard deviations for all 2222 crystal entries compared. Exact diagonalization of the same 2424-site Hamiltonians gives E0/N=−0.448329E_{0}/N=-0.448329, −0.538598-0.538598, and −0.712710-0.712710 at A0, C1a, and C1b, below every projected energy on that cluster. On this torus, the smallest compatible with the 2×22\times 2 cells of cuboc1 and of the crystal, the J+J_{+} bonds coincide pairwise, so that these energies do not represent the cross-octagon model. The next compatible cluster has 4848 sites.

Fits. Energies are extrapolated linearly in 1/N1/N by weighted least squares, with the error scaled by χ2/ν\sqrt{\chi^{2}/\nu} where it exceeds one. For the ordered state χ2/ν\chi^{2}/\nu lies between 0.10.1 and 11, whereas for the crystal and the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} states it reaches 10210^{2} to 10310^{3}: their energies scatter between clusters by 10−310^{-3} to 10−210^{-2}, beyond their statistical errors, which reflects the several local minima of their optimization rather than a finite-size law. We distinguish three uncertainties. The statistical errors of the twist-averaged energies are 0.50.5 to 3×10−43\times 10^{-4} per site. Optimizations from different starting points can end in different local minima. We keep the lowest, so that this uncertainty is one-sided. Where two starts were run, they agree within 1.5×10−41.5\times 10^{-4} for the crystal at λ=0.4\lambda=0.4, 0.450.45, and 0.50.5 on 216216 sites, but differ by 5×10−35\times 10^{-3} to 9×10−39\times 10^{-3} at λ=0.3\lambda=0.3 and 0.350.35, and by up to 0.040.04 on the cut at J+=1J_{+}=1. The extrapolation adds the spread over fit forms. Table S7 therefore lists the differences on the largest common cluster next to the extrapolations. Alternative fit forms, linear in 1/L1/L, the mean of the two largest clusters, and the largest cluster, give the ranges shown in Fig. 9 of the main text.

Chirality of the class-ℬ\mathcal{B} ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} state. Table S8 gives the scalar chirality of ℬ\mathcal{B}:Z000-111 near the crossing. The projected chirality ⟨𝑺i⋅(𝑺j×𝑺k)⟩\langle\bm{S}_{i}\cdot(\bm{S}_{j}\times\bm{S}_{k})\rangle on the nearest-neighbor triangles is uniform, with staggered components below 2×10−32\times 10^{-3}, and decreases with the cluster size at each λ\lambda. The optimized amplitudes themselves are only weakly chiral: the time-reversal-odd part sin⁡Φ△=Im⁡tr⁡P/(2​|detP|1/2)\sin\Phi_{\triangle}=\operatorname{Im}\operatorname{tr}P/(2|\det P|^{1/2}) of the loop operator P=ui​j​uj​k​uk​iP=u_{ij}u_{jk}u_{ki} of a triangle is at most 0.10.1, compared with 11 for ℬ\mathcal{B}:SU011-001 and 00 for the TRS states, and at λ=0.5\lambda=0.5 it decreases with the cluster size as well.

Jastrow factor of the ordered state. A Jastrow factor exp⁡(∑cvc​∑⟨i​j⟩∈cSi′z​Sj′z)\exp(\sum_{c}v_{c}\sum_{\langle ij\rangle\in c}S^{\prime z}_{i}S^{\prime z}_{j}) in the local frame of the order, in which the quantization axis of site ii is 𝒏i\bm{n}_{i}, with one parameter on each of the bond orbits J1J_{1}, J23J_{23}, J×J_{\times}, and J+J_{+}, was optimized on top of the ordered determinant. It lowers the ordered energy by (5,3,1)×10−4(5,3,1)\times 10^{-4} at λ=0.35\lambda=0.35, (6,9,5)×10−4(6,9,5)\times 10^{-4} at λ=0.4\lambda=0.4, (10,9,8)×10−4(10,9,8)\times 10^{-4} at λ=0.45\lambda=0.45, (11,9,10)×10−4(11,9,10)\times 10^{-4} at C1a, and (2,23,17)×10−4(2,23,17)\times 10^{-4} at C1b, on 9696, 216216, and 384384 sites, and m2m^{2} by 0.0010.001 to 0.0140.014. The extrapolated difference between the best spin liquid and the ordered state at λ=0.35\lambda=0.35 remains compatible with zero, +0.0005​(3)+0.0005(3), so that their crossing is unchanged, and the extrapolated energies of the crystal and the ordered state at C1a become equal within the errors. An Sz​SzS^{z}S^{z} factor breaks the spin-rotation symmetry of the singlet states and was not applied to them.

Nematic chiral state. The time-reversal-breaking state N:Z00000-110 of the nematic class of cuboc1 was optimized on 216216 sites at C1a, C1c (J+=0.8J_{+}=0.8, J×=0.3J_{\times}=0.3), and C1d (J+=0.3J_{+}=0.3, J×=0.8J_{\times}=0.8) and measured on 384384 sites with one boundary condition: E/N=−0.41871​(11)E/N=-0.41871(11), −0.42015​(12)-0.42015(12), and −0.41989​(10)-0.41989(10), against −0.44453​(9)-0.44453(9), −0.46593​(11)-0.46593(11), and −0.46678​(12)-0.46678(12) for the lowest projected spin liquid at these points in the same protocol.

Valence-bond crystal. Figure S3 shows the nearest-neighbor correlations of the crystal at λ=0.4\lambda=0.4 and at C1a. Strong square–bow-tie dimers, with ⟨𝑺i⋅𝑺j⟩≈−0.68\langle\bm{S}_{i}\cdot\bm{S}_{j}\rangle\approx-0.68 to −0.70-0.70, form pinwheels around half of the squares, and the other squares resonate. The pattern is the same at both couplings.

Appendix SX Projective Symmetry Groups of the Nematic Class

The nematic subgroup p​2​m​mp2mm of p​4​m​mp4mm is generated by T1T_{1}, T2T_{2}, and the axial mirrors σx:(X,Y)→(−X,Y)\sigma_{x}:(X,Y)\to(-X,Y) and σy:(X,Y)→(X,−Y)\sigma_{y}:(X,Y)\to(X,-Y) through the square center, σx=σ​C4−1\sigma_{x}=\sigma C_{4}^{-1} and σy=σ​C4\sigma_{y}=\sigma C_{4} in terms of the generators of Sec. II of the main text. Their product is the twofold rotation C42C_{4}^{2}. The group p​2​m​m×ℤ2Θp2mm\times\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{\Theta} is defined by the thirteen relations

T2​T1​T2−1​T1−1=σx​T1​σx−1​T1=σx​T2​σx−1​T2−1=e,\displaystyle T_{2}T_{1}T_{2}^{-1}T_{1}^{-1}=\sigma_{x}T_{1}\sigma_{x}^{-1}T_{1}=\sigma_{x}T_{2}\sigma_{x}^{-1}T_{2}^{-1}=e,
σy​T1​σy−1​T1−1=σy​T2​σy−1​T2=e,\displaystyle\sigma_{y}T_{1}\sigma_{y}^{-1}T_{1}^{-1}=\sigma_{y}T_{2}\sigma_{y}^{-1}T_{2}=e,
σx2=σy2=(σx​σy)2=Θ2=e,\displaystyle\sigma_{x}^{2}=\sigma_{y}^{2}=(\sigma_{x}\sigma_{y})^{2}=\Theta^{2}=e,
O​Θ​O−1​Θ−1=e(O=T1,T2,σx,σy).\displaystyle O\,\Theta\,O^{-1}\Theta^{-1}=e\quad(O=T_{1},T_{2},\sigma_{x},\sigma_{y}). (S9)

Every generator occurs an even number of times in every relator, so that all 1616 sign assignments to (T1,T2,σx,σy)(T_{1},T_{2},\sigma_{x},\sigma_{y}) are characters, and re-liftings never change a relation value. We label a ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} PSG ZnT2​nx​T1​nx​T2​ny​T1​ny​T2n_{T_{2}}n_{xT_{1}}n_{xT_{2}}n_{yT_{1}}n_{yT_{2}}-nx​ny​nx​yn_{x}n_{y}n_{xy}, where a digit 11 marks the value −1-1 of, in this order, the relations T2​T1​T2−1​T1−1T_{2}T_{1}T_{2}^{-1}T_{1}^{-1}, σx​T1​σx−1​T1\sigma_{x}T_{1}\sigma_{x}^{-1}T_{1}, σx​T2​σx−1​T2−1\sigma_{x}T_{2}\sigma_{x}^{-1}T_{2}^{-1}, σy​T1​σy−1​T1−1\sigma_{y}T_{1}\sigma_{y}^{-1}T_{1}^{-1}, σy​T2​σy−1​T2\sigma_{y}T_{2}\sigma_{y}^{-1}T_{2}, σx2\sigma_{x}^{2}, σy2\sigma_{y}^{2}, and (σx​σy)2(\sigma_{x}\sigma_{y})^{2}. The S​U​(2)SU(2) PSGs carry the same digits after SU, and a U⁡(1)U(1) PSG is labeled UwT1​wT2​wσx​wσyw_{T_{1}}w_{T_{2}}w_{\sigma_{x}}w_{\sigma_{y}}-nn, where wO=1w_{O}=1 marks the operations that reverse the U⁡(1)U(1) rotation and nn is an index, as for p​4​m​mp4mm. The character of cuboc1, read off from its spin configuration, is ϵ⁡(T1,T2,σx,σy)=(−,+,+,+)\epsilon(T_{1},T_{2},\sigma_{x},\sigma_{y})=(-,+,+,+): the translation T1T_{1} is combined with time reversal, and the mirror x→a−Xx\to a-X, T1​σxT_{1}\sigma_{x}, also has ϵ=−1\epsilon=-1.

Under p​2​m​mp2mm the four square sites form one orbit at the general position, and the bow-tie sites 55 and 66 form two separate orbits, at the positions (a/2,0)(a/2,0) and (0,a/2)(0,a/2), each with site symmetry 2​m​m2mm. The twelve bond orbits of p​4​m​mp4mm up to J+J_{+} split into 2121: JdJ_{d}, Jb​bJ_{bb}, and J×J_{\times} do not split, and each of the other nine splits into two orbits related by C4C_{4}, with bonds along xx and along yy. In particular the horizontal and vertical square edges are inequivalent, and the bow-tie edges split into the legs to site 55 and those to site 66, each mixing the orbits J2J_{2} and J3J_{3} of the model with inequivalent bow-tie edges.

The ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} PSGs follow as in Sec. SII. Of the 256256 classes of H2​(p​2​m​m,ℤ2)H^{2}(p2mm,\mathbb{Z}_{2}), 100100 are realizable on the three site orbits, each with exactly one PSG, since the characters act transitively on the four sign representations of each 2​m​m2mm bow-tie orbit and the square orbit has trivial site symmetry. There are 44 S​U​(2)SU(2) PSGs and 4848 discrete U⁡(1)U(1) PSGs, with one flux family in the sector in which both mirrors reverse the U⁡(1)U(1) rotation and the translations do not. As for p​4​m​mp4mm, the algebraic PSGs are the same for all 1616 characters, which enter only through the realization. Table S9 gives the realized counts for the character of cuboc1. The half-square chirality of cuboc1 needs the JdJ_{d} bonds and is reproduced by 5858 ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} and 77 U⁡(1)U(1) PSGs. The full chirality pattern at graph distance two, over 1111 chiral loop orbits, is reproduced by 2424 ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} and 33 U⁡(1)U(1) PSGs, 1717 of which also reproduce its 66 vanishing loop orbits. The pattern over all 1919 chiral loop orbits up to J+J_{+} is reproduced by 2424 ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} and 22 U⁡(1)U(1) PSGs. The combination T1​ΘT_{1}\Theta reverses the Hall response, so every state of this class has C=0C=0 and κx​y=0\kappa_{xy}=0.
